en: Salutation to the venerable Guru Śiva. Salutation to the one served by the illustrious, illustrious, and illustrious [deities]. May there be well-being.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇanātha! Oṃ! To the one who experiences the majesty of the supreme sovereignty consisting of light and awareness, which is glorious, auspicious, self-sovereign, unconditioned, and undivided...

O King of Kings, you are victorious as this very Supreme Śiva— intoxicated by the non-dual supreme bliss that is innate, natural, and renowned; the sovereign of the empire of the ever-arising supreme power, whose universal vibration has dawned.
Oṃ! Homage be to Maheśvara, who is supreme, whose sovereignty is uniquely skilled in encompassing all within his own self, who dwells beyond, and who is both the self and the non-self.
By those who dwell in the state of Sahib Kaul— who possess mastery over the injunctions to be grasped through the worship of their own wish-fulfilling tree—
the state of the Self is realized as being very near.

Here indeed, by the command of the heart of the Great King named Yameva, the sovereign of the specific region of Maruvāṭa— who was captivated by the request of one named Siṃha— the Sāhibakaula, who manifested himself in the excellent land of Kaśmīra, composed this *Snārāsa*.

By designating a certain state of stability as the "Bond of the Wish-fulfilling Tree," this slight effort is made to establish that the views of the Non-dual Brahman, the Non-dual Śiva, and the Great Non-dual [traditions] constitute the established tenets of all philosophical systems.
It was composed for the purpose of instructing the ignorant; for this very reason, there is an avoidance of Sanskrit words with hidden meanings.
Among those three great views:
The ultimate truth consists precisely in the demonstration of non-duality among all great philosophical systems;
however, even therein, the specific tenets of each respective school have also been set forth.
This effort [of the author] was undertaken for the purpose of removing contradictions regarding those specific points.
In this regard, first is the introduction beginning with "The venerable Śrīguhya-svatantra," and so forth.

Herein is the meaning: You are made manifest through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and are eternally present before one's eyes; you have been directly realized at the very same moment as one's own experience.

By the word "self" (svayam), the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is meant as "I. Just as those standing on this shore repeatedly call the other shore "this shore," while those standing on that shore perceive their "this shore" as the "other shore" and their "other shore" as the "this shore."
Just as a single human being is the son of his father, the father of his son,
the father-in-law of his daughter-in-law, and the son-in-law of his father-in-law—
thus consisting of various relations yet remaining one and the same— so too is it with the two words "thou" and "I."
The state of being mutual synonyms.

The notion of "I" arises for oneself with respect to oneself, while for another, that same status is established through the cognition of being addressed as such; this is because one is presented by another through the verbal expression "you. This very point has been determined in the *Vāsiṣṭha* regarding yoga: "You and I."
Regarding the passage beginning with "by the two words," etc.:

Paramaśiva is "supreme" (paramaḥ) because his supreme liberation-glory (mokṣalakṣmī) is unsurpassed; he protects (pipatti) by means of the essence of his own "I-ness" (svāhaṃtā), [extending] from Anāśrita and the rest down to the Earth (mahī). His nature is absolute freedom (svātantrya).
It fulfills the manifold manifestation of the universe. [As stated in texts such as: "The Supreme, having created that very thing, entered into that very thing," and so forth;
and "Having entered by means of this living self," and so forth.
Therefore, based on the Vedic scripture stating, "From this Self, space was produced," and so forth,

as well as the Śaiva scripture stating, "The enjoyer alone exists everywhere at all times in the form of the object of enjoyment," I know [all] through the self of Sadāśiva; or rather, he knows me through his own self.
Thus, according to the venerable Mahāguru Śrī Somānanda Pāda and others:

that very [reality] nourishes and protects its own nature; having manifested by itself within itself through its own self, it shines as consisting of light and reflective awareness (prakāśa-vimarśa) through the contemplation of its own essential nature.

Or, another [explanation] is that he "fashions" (vidadhāti), and thus he is *apara*. He is *ma* because he measures (*māti*) and thoroughly measures (*pramāti*)—that is, by virtue of being the independent agent, he contemplates within himself this very [reality] which consists of non-difference from his own essential nature.
He is *para* and he is *ma*, hence *parama*; for according to such scriptural passages as "the object is indeed beyond the senses," he is supreme.

Or, it is "para-ma" because he is determined as the Supreme (para) and he is "I" (ma). Furthermore, he measures out (minoti), casts aside, or distances the "other" (param)—that is, the second—thus he is the "Supreme" (parama), being without a second. Or, he is "supreme" (parama) because at the time of direct experience, he perceives that the "other"—namely the body, senses, and so forth—"does not exist. [He measures out] the other, such as the body and so on.
He desires; or, at the time of his own ignorance, he exchanges [his nature], or he interchanges by means of the conceit of being his own self—thus he is *parama*.

Or, at the occasion of the desire to emit the supreme *paranāda*, he causes it to sound, or he brings about its state of being the object of his own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*)—thus he is *parama*. Furthermore...
Through the secret non-dual vision, that supreme darkness is he;

and he is the conscious letter *ma*. Since the letter *ma* is of two kinds—conscious and unconscious—the final letter of the *pa*-group (*ma*) is the conscious one. However, that which consists of the fifteen vowels and the *anusvāra* is the other.

The conscious one is the meaning of *bindu*; he alone is Paramaśiva. This is because of the *Śivasūkti*: "I am the *bindu*, you are the *visarga*. The meaning is that Śiva is the essence of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the absolute "I-ness" (*ahantā*) of Śiva; "Śiva" means one who is free from all remaining afflictions (*upadrava*).
"It is from this very bliss that other [limited] forms of bliss derive their existence. "Who indeed could breathe, who could live, if there were no inquiry into this bliss?
And according to the Śruti passage beginning with "He is indeed rasa," [bliss] is distinct from the various other forms of bliss derived from wealth, sons, and so forth.

You are Śiva, the Supreme; you are victorious! You are auspicious, characterized by consciousness and bliss; you blow [the breath of life], grant, and bestow [liberation] upon those to be graced who are non-different from yourself, merely by the dissolution of the delusion imagined by them, thereby manifesting [yourself]. You are both supreme and Śiva—thus, Paramaśiva. You are victorious!

It exists as the most excellent of all. For indeed, he who is the most excellent is also one to whom everyone bows. Just as when a king or someone else of supreme excellence is traveling on a road, if one fails to offer him salutation, it results in one's own ruin and madness.
"May there be no harm whatsoever"—thus we have offered salutations to Him, our own Great Lord (Maheśvara).

This very path is the one followed by all expressions such as "victory" (*jaya*) and so forth. Now, in the non-dualist (*advaita*) system, since nothing remains after [the realization of] the Self, how can the act of salutation be possible, and for whom or by what means?
If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of duality, that is true;
however, [the term "prahva"] follows the meaning of the verbal root *ṇama* (to bow).

Having cast beneath our feet the predominance of the conceit of the body and so forth, we have attained immersion into that [divine essence]; this is the meaning expressed by the act of salutation. But what is the nature of this "You"? You are both the possessor of glory (*śrīmān*) and glory itself (*śrī*).
And he is completely autonomous, independent, and partless; he consists of supreme light and self-awareness (*prakāśa-vimarśa*); he is the experiencer of the power of supreme sovereignty;
and he is the universal vibration (*spanda*) of the non-dual existence that is innate, natural, and filled with the highest bliss.

He is one who possesses Śrī— meaning power, splendor, and the supreme fortune that removes the wretchedness of the contraction of knowledge— and he is one for whom those very qualities are abundant (bhūman). He is *tā*.

He who possesses such praise, and he who possesses constant union with those very [qualities]. Or, "Śrīmān" means one who churns away *śrī*—the splendor known as *saṃsāra*; and he is that [very person], for at the time of his own realization, the nature of *saṃsāra* appears as splendor.

Because it is manifest, He Himself is Śrī; He is the embodiment of that triad, perfectly independent—the divider within non-duality and the non-divider through internal synthesis within that which has been divided.
This means He is the bearer of the great royal insignia, not looking toward the faces of others for support.

For this very reason, although the Anāśrita exists within the sixfold aspects of the subject (*pramātṛkalā*), it always remains transcending them; for this same reason, it is partless (*nirbhāga*). Indeed, the division of parts is not possible for the Anāśrita, because it is itself indivisible.
Because it would result in contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "Who saw the first-born being born boneless, since he is divided by bones?
and "As one who seeks to overstep his own shadow with his feet."
For it is stated in the secret teaching: "The head should not be above [the body], for such is this Vaindavīkalā.
Therefore, that which consists of supreme light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the Supreme Lordship (*pārameśvaryam*);
its *anubhāva* is its greatness, and those who possess that greatness are its *anubhāvakas*.

He is the one who brings about the experience of that [Reality]; he is celebrated among them as being manifest, unassisted, ancient, honored, eternal, and his own; and he is the innate, non-different from himself, vibration of the universal existence of non-dual supreme bliss, as previously determined.

Now, when the analysis of the very substantive "Paramaśiva" has been performed, these qualifiers such as "Śrīmat" and so forth follow by the force of the context itself. Once they have followed by the force of the context, there is no need to state them again, nor is there any purpose in subsequently stating other supplementary sentences.
If it is argued that this leads to the fault of tautology, we say no; for this one and only Great Lord of His own Self,
being expounded through hundreds of great discourses, [is revealed] to those who possess the power of His grace.

"In whatever way possible, it comes into direct manifestation. Thus, that very reality of Brahman, which has been expounded again and again by the Vedas and other scriptures, and which will be determined in many ways due to its nature as possessing infinite powers, ascends to the path of inquiry.

Furthermore, because it causes the accumulation of impurities and the cycle of birth and death throughout millions of various lifetimes, this single [principle] has been—and continues to be—repeatedly established; thus, even when restated, it does not entail redundancy.
For this very reason, the doctrines of Bṛhaspati and others are refuted by these qualifying attributes. Since:
Whatever consists of light is, by its very nature, beyond extension and is nothing other than one's own essential being.

That which is non-luminous, however, while undergoing a state of non-existence by itself, is incapable of performing any action for another. For this very reason, it has been sung in the venerable *Pratyabhijñā-śāstra*:
Regarding the phrases "in the agent," "in the knower," and so forth, the refutation of those [views] will become clear further on;
therefore, nothing more is elaborated here. Furthermore, what is it like? It is that which has arisen from "that" (tad), meaning it has arisen most intensely.

That by which movement has been transcended and traversed because of its all-pervasiveness; that whose knowledge is thus moved; that which is arisen, eternally arisen, and devoid of the states of creation and so forth;
that whose sovereign empire of supreme power is non-different from itself—for indeed, [it is] Paramaśiva.
It is never devoid of power (*niśśakti*).

For if it were devoid of power, the creation and other cosmic processes would lack a foundation; nor should it be suspected that if it were always possessed of power, liberation could not be attained due to the constant existence of creation and the rest—this is because [the power] operates only within the context of creation and so forth.

Everything of that [consciousness] is always real, because bondage arises through the failure to recognize the true nature of all entities as being one's own self; and even when those entities are non-existent, there is the manifestation of the non-difference between power and the possessor of power through the synthesis of their essential form within the supreme power itself.
Furthermore, what kind of being is the King? Kings are the mind, intellect, individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth;
their kings are the great souls (*mahājīvas*) who possess the conceit of being Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and the like; he is the Lord (*īśvara*) of even them, because they too—

By attaining even a drop of the supreme glory consisting of that [Lord's] light and self-awareness, they have become Supreme Lords; what more need be said of him who is the Great Lord of all? He himself, within himself, is clear through the self-reflection (*vimarśa*) of his own light, which is the realization of his own nature.

Furthermore, luminosity itself attains the state of self-reflection (*vimarśatva*). Because it is distinguished from other forms of luminosity through the contemplation of self-luminosity as taught in the scriptures and other sources, luminosity that has not attained self-reflection is indeed non-luminous, as it is incapable of performing any function. Now, [the objection]:
Even that which is non-luminous is indeed luminous, because it is manifested precisely as non-luminous;
for without luminosity, even the attribute called "luminosity" would not be perceived.
Likewise, even ignorance is indeed knowledge, because it is [manifested] in the form of ignorance.
Because it is an object of knowledge, it is not distinct from cognition.

Oṃ! Of that very Ma, which manifests through its own sovereignty, she is the seed-syllable consisting of the complete accumulation of all things, characterized by the excellence of supreme innate *ahaṃtā*.

This is indeed that one, unique, infinite, and unsurpassed consciousness, consisting of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with the pure ten-fold powers, which is the radiance of the jewel of infinite power accompanied by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the triad beginning with Paśyantī in the form of a trident; it is the illuminator of its own infinite, supreme, and all-surpassing play.

That [Power], which bestows the nectar of the innate vitality (*sahaja-ojas*)— the supreme reality consisting of the three transcended states (*tattva-tīrṇātṛka*)— is intent upon the arising of the vibration of supreme joy through the breaking of the limbs of the body;
it is the opening and closing, the unfolding and folding, of the various powers of Maheśvara.
The Great Power, known as Parā, though transcending all things, is nevertheless fully manifest as everything itself, having emerged intensely from the unfolding of ultimate reality.

Because this very previously determined Supreme Śiva possesses the essence of non-difference from the aforementioned Supreme Śiva, it is "proceeded" (*prakrāntā*); likewise, because it is well-known among those who possess knowledge and among those who are the opposite,
it is "well-established" (*prasiddhā*), being known and unknown respectively by the knowers and their opposites.

And it has been experienced through direct perception. If it is asked: "Since it is known by those possessing knowledge (*jñānin*), yet not known by those who are ignorant of reality due to their distorted views, how can it be said to have been 'experienced'? It is replied: Even one who possesses knowledge, when saying "I recognize him" or "I recognize her," certainly knows [it].

Because I am manifested as non-different from the light that reflects upon my own state, I am indeed the Knower who experiences reality as it truly is; whereas the ignorant person, though perceiving through the distortion of identifying with the body and so forth,
still perceives [the Self] precisely because of its nature as indivisible light.

Because it has as its essence the non-differentiation from all things, the reflective awareness such as "I know," which consists of pure consciousness (*vimarśamayatva*), cannot otherwise be explained except through the loss of its own [limited] nature; thus,
this supreme power (*parā*) is experienced as non-different from You.
For you, though one, there is a second name— just like the moon and its moonlight—
which is called "Parā" because it is proclaimed on all sides by the Supreme Lord (Para),
and whose renown (khyāti) is supreme, and whose very essence is the Supreme Lord himself.
She whose name is proclaimed from herself to others— that is, to great living beings—

and who proclaims (ākhyāti), that is, reveals, the supreme Self (param) which has been determined by the intellect; she whose names are distinct as "supreme" (parā) and "inferior" (aparā), and who possesses whatever names there may be.
The meaning is that all those things prescribed for her by the great ones do not establish her true purpose,
but were merely devised for the sake of worldly convention because she is devoid of destruction; for this very reason,
she is "Mahāśakti"— that which is both great and the supreme power.

The power of His own manifestation is non-different from Himself. Furthermore, according to the perspective of the secret doctrine, this "great incapacity" is not a lack of power, but rather Śiva Himself. Through His own blinking—that is, through the unfolding of His own manifestation—the reflective awareness of the supreme I-consciousness (*aham*) arises; it is of that very [consciousness]...

And at the moment when the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) [of the subject] closes its own manifestation, it occurs through a reversal by means of its own opening (*unmeṣa*), which is called "orientation toward itself" (*svonmukhatā*). Furthermore, the reflective awareness is expressed as "the Great One" (*mahā*).
And that very power (*śakti*) is present here, distinguished by the analysis of the phonemes *śa* and *va*.
The reflective awareness "I" (*aham*) arises through the combination of the initial *a* and the final *ha*, resulting in the formation of the *anusvāra* (*-m*). Now, one might object:
from the perspective of grammatical science, there is proximity between the letters *a* and *ha*, yet from another perspective...

If it is argued that the mutual proximity of the *varga*-initials (the gutturals, etc. and the *ka*-series (the consonants beginning with *ka*) is appropriate because they are situated nearby, whereas such is not the case for the letters *a* and *ha*, which appear extremely distant due to their positions as the first and last [of their respective series];

True; however, in this context, it is appropriate that only the vowels (ākāra) and the consonant *ha* are in proximity and form a mutual aggregate, because the *mātrikā* appears as a garland consisting of fifty letters. For instance:
In a garland, the second bead or any other subsequent bead does not possess the same degree of conjunction as the first and the last beads;
therefore, by the rule of their union, the letters *a* and *ha* alone are most intimately proximate.
There is no coexistence of one color with another color;

rather, it is only within the aggregate of these two that there is the supreme and subordinate reflective awareness (*parāparāmarśa*) as "I," according to the scriptural injunctions such as "I alone existed in the beginning" and "Being alone existed in the beginning. This [awareness] is the delusion of reflection, thinking "this is I."

And the teachings of Pratyabhijñā [state]: "That very Parā, by abandoning her own orientation [toward herself], becomes oriented toward Śiva; she is the Great One, the great abode of reflective awareness (parāmarśa). And that very same [Parā] is the power (śakti) consisting of Paraśiva himself, which is the Great One as the reconnection with one's own state."

Or it is victorious by means of the preceding recurrence; here, the connection is "it is seated in this very [place]," and the genitive case also reveals this very relationship between Śiva and Śakti. According to the statement in the *Śivasūtravimarśinī*, "the state of the conscious is consciousness" (*caitanya*), as in the expression "the head of Rāhu" or "the tail of Ketu."
It is like [the expressions] "ask" and so forth, and not like "the son of the father" and so forth. For you,
how could there be independence for this very [Self] while it is undergoing a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) within its own created, non-different, and self-manifested glory—
as in the case of the analogies of the rope-snake and so forth— for those whose minds are shrouded by delusion imagined by themselves?

Of that which is manifesting. And this very [reality] is the specific object of each respective view—namely, the non-dual Brahman and the non-dual Śiva—and not of one another. For what has been determined as the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) by the proponents of non-dual Brahman, and as the doctrine of absolute freedom (*svātantryavāda*) by the proponents of non-dual Śiva, is [unified] by this [work].

We have demonstrated through our discourse how that Maheśvara does not undergo transformation (vivarta) into any other distinct category of object; rather, having manifested His own sovereign power in the form of absolute freedom,
He Himself transforms into those very objects as if they were His own mental constructs.
For those who possess veils and for those who possess His grace, that [reality] shines forth by means of the removal of those veils;

having abandoned the cognition of distinctions such as the "lower" (apara) and so forth, it shines all the more intensely as consisting solely of self-luminous reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), for nothing whatsoever can [obstruct] the Supreme Lord.
There is a state of difference, by which it appears here as a form of manifestation (*vivarta*) belonging to one thing as if it were another;
yet, because its own essence consists of self-luminous awareness (*vimarśa*), it entirely abandons such manifestation through the power of its own grace for those who are to be graced.

Brahman alone, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, liberated, supreme bliss, and non-dual, manifests; and having abandoned the notion of independence [of the individual], that very One alone shines forth as the unconditioned and independent. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the two.

Because the application [of the argument] is precisely for the purpose of establishing ultimate identity, even further on, the intended meaning is that their mutual non-difference should be understood as the exclusion of each respective specific attribute;
in this sense, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of subsistence (*sthiti*) and so forth, as well as the entirety [of the characteristics], is intended.

That supreme innate I-consciousness (*parama-sahajāhaṃtā*), which is the seed of the provisions, sustenance, and so forth for the venerable Lord Ananta who is the form of Viṣṇu—how has it become such that it remains as nothing else? It is both supreme and innate;
it is supreme by virtue of its identity with the Supreme Other, and it is innate by virtue of its non-difference from Śiva.

Furthermore, what is the specific nature of that "I-ness" (ahantā)? It is that very "I-ness" which, because it possesses the forms of superior, middling, and inferior, remains as the residue even when everything—
from the "teeth" (dantādi) onwards— is dissolved in states such as deep sleep or at the time of cosmic dissolution.
The meaning is that "I-ness" (ahantā) alone is thus intended. Furthermore, "I-ness" itself is the distinction (*viśeṣa*).

The intended sense is: that in which there is no remainder (*vigataśeṣa*), and wherein even the state of being a remainder (*śeṣabhāva*) has ceased; moreover, he is both "without remainder" (*vigataśeṣa*) and "the remainder" (*śeṣa*)—that remainder which is devoid of all states such as "remainder" (*śeṣa*) and so forth.

Non-ego itself is its "remainder" (śeṣa); furthermore, the remainder of the remainders is the "remainder-of-remainders" (śeṣaśeṣa). That from which the remainder-of-remainders has departed is "devoid-of-remainder-of-remainders" (viśeṣaśeṣa). Non-ego itself is the "remainder-of-remainders" (viśeṣaśeṣa) belonging to that [state]. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the seed-nature for the fulfillment of the entire collection [of merit and knowledge], and thus it is not a mere "remainder" (aśeṣa).

For those whose manifestations of Śiva are always complete and unimpeded, there is the bearing—that is, the sustaining—of the weight of the entire collection (*parikara*) whose purpose is the great goal;
those for whom this is primary are the "seed-Śivas" (*vījaśiva*), who are the seeds of creation. This refers to the initial stage of emanation.

Although the inclusion of dissolution, concealment, and grace is logically appropriate as the first [category] alongside emanation in the context of the material cause (*upādāna*), they are presented first because of the primacy of persistence (*sthiti*) itself, since it consists of the manifestation of those very processes beginning with emanation.

The mention of "that very [power]" refers to the totality of the equipment (saṃbhāra) of Śiva alone—the phenomenal universe extending from the self (svātman) down to the earth. It is the primary seed for the maintenance of that universe.
This is so even though, in relation to the lower levels, other beings such as Īśvara and the rest also possess the nature of seeds.

The meaning is that, by virtue of its predominance, she alone is the seed; furthermore, she is the "repository" (sambhāra) of all things—that is to say, the womb-dwelling (garbhanivāsa) for creation. In that context, "bearing" (bharaṇa) means nourishing; the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "for the sake of the self which is the seed and so forth" includes subsistence and the other [stages of existence]. Moreover—

Because she is the nature of the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*), which serves as the seed for the accumulation of the provisions for the entire Lord Ananta Bhaṭṭāraka, who is the form of Viṣṇu; furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is "in the form of a trident," and so forth—meaning that although her single form was initially [unmanifest], it has now [become manifest] at the front in the shape of a trident.
And that triad, consisting of Paśyantī and the others, exists in a state of differentiation; its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the Great Light (*mahas*).
Those who possess this [awareness] as their friend (*sakha*)—or those who are similar to it—are like the radiance of the light of those jewels of infinite power. It is their luminous manifestation.

Its manifestation is its state of being slightly manifest (*kacitatva*). Its state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) is its state of being of one flavor (*samarasatva*), meaning that, like the absence of waves within a windless ocean, the manifestations of all powers—beginning with *paśyantī* and ending with *sakalā*—abide as if within the Supreme (*parā*) alone; this is what is meant.

That which is most excellent belongs to Him; for, by virtue of the manifestation of infinite powers (*ananta-śakti*), the triad beginning with Paśyantī alone is His companion—capable of manifesting those respective forms because the essence of all powers is non-different from that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). By means of this state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*), [He acts].

It is indicated that even at the time when all powers have ceased entirely, the residence remains within the womb of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), and not a dissolution (*pralaya*) synonymous with the destruction of those respective powers. Now, if all powers were indestructible, the state of worldly existence (*bhava*) would necessarily persist forever, leading to the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*).

If this is argued, we say no; for the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) is precisely our doctrine, since "I" and "we" are [the very nature of] that [Self].

If He were devoid of power, even names such as "Śiva" and so forth would be impossible to establish. For at the moment when powers manifest through His own unfolding, there occurs a synthesis of various names and forms; yet, through the withdrawal of those powers, [He remains as He is].

Because, with respect to the intention of [Śiva’s] own manifestation, there is no conceptualization of various names and so forth; and because even in the state of possessing power (*śaktimattā*), since it is non-different from Śiva, the undesirable consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa*) does not arise.
Furthermore, in these monistic systems (*advaitadarśana*), bondage and liberation are ultimately identical in their true nature.

It is precisely at the moment of one's own conceptualization and delusion that dualism and other such constructs arise through imagination, attaining existence for only a moment like objects in a dream; and upon the departure of that [delusion], there is liberation through the realization of the ultimate reality as it truly is.

Since everything, including liberation and so forth, is merely an illusion consisting solely of one's own mental construction, what then is consciousness? It is that which consists of the essence of self-reflection (*svavimarśa*) in the form of pure awareness (*caitanya*). For this very reason, it is everywhere one and the same in its nature as consciousness, because there is no obstruction. But is it not [the case] in the non-inert (*ajaḍa*)...?

If it is argued that being of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpatva*) is invariable [in the case of the Self], whereas in the case of the insentient (*jaḍa*) it is variable, we reply: First, it is already established that the non-insentient is indeed of the nature of consciousness. Furthermore, although the insentient is itself unconscious, it is nonetheless non-insentient because it is perceived as an object by that which is of the nature of consciousness.

Because it cannot be the object of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as something distinct from that [consciousness], it would follow that it lacks luminosity (*aprakāśatva*); and because it lacks connection with the nature of existence (*sadrūpatā*), it is "non-existent" (*amata*). Thus, since even its own designation as an insentient entity (*jaḍa*) and so forth is utterly impossible to maintain, for this very reason the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "here there is only one" excludes any other connection.

It is precisely for this reason that there is a certain indefinable [power] which is to be realized through one's own experience; since Paramaśiva is not definable due to his being untouched by duality, the Supreme Power (paraśakti) is likewise indefinable, as she is of the same nature as him.

Regarding the scriptural passages such as "by the single essence of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana eva*) and "where indeed there is duality alone," one might object: since both [consciousness and the world] are equally indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), and since [the world] is pervasive and eternal, a contradiction would arise because they would possess mutually exclusive desires for action and non-action. To this, we reply: no.

Because it expresses the number two merely by name, yet in reality consists of the nature of a single category (*padārtha*), it is manifold in its many ways: in the state of unfolding (*unmeṣa*), it is of the nature of power (*śakti*) due to its differentiation (*kalana*); and in the state of closing (*nimeṣa*), it is the remainder of the very nature of Śiva.
Because that reality has been determined previously and is being determined even now, for this very reason it is infinite;
since its time of origin is beginningless, it is all the more utterly free from destruction. Furthermore, it is an infinite certainty, as everything is one's own self.
Because they are always equal in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), and because doubt and the like—
though commonly accepted as such— are in fact not so accepted; for one who does not know their true nature as the Self at any time is surely a laughingstock to the Knower of the Self.

Because he possesses a body, the knower is merely an object of laughter for one who knows; for it is by knowing what is unknown that a person achieves human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). What human purpose, indeed, is there in knowing what is already known?
If it is argued that, in this case, the teachings of the scriptures and so forth would be useless, we say no, because [the truth] has not yet reached one's own throat.

Just as one who has forgotten their ornaments [is restored to them], the result for them is merely the removal of delusion; for there is the Śruti: "Whose [it was], his it remains," and so forth, and the Smṛti:
"As it was, so it remains," and so forth. Furthermore, what is it? It is not that.

For it is more excellent because, just as the various other principles (tattvas) do not initially grant entry into the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava, so too they do not enhance consciousness as much as the accomplishments of states (bhāva-siddhis) do;
yet even those do not enhance it as much as the supreme, perfectly full consciousness of Bhairava does.
And its manifestation is itself unrestrained and independent, because its essence consists in honor.

There is no further answer in the form of a response. For this reason, when the disciple has been made to overflow with the boundless radiance of infinite creative intuition (*pratibhā*) arising from the surging ocean of Great Consciousness (*mahāsaṃvit*), he becomes a fit vessel for question and answer; that alone is, in reality, the truth.
What else could be more unsurpassed than this, the teacher’s own teaching, which is "constantly manifest"? || 2 ||
The "crossing over" (uttaraṇa) is the "supreme" (uttara), which is liberation as conceived by the proponents of dualism; for that [liberation] is in reality fixed,
having first established itself upon the ground of the body, vital breath, and so forth, and having ascended to the stage of the Void (śūnyapada), it rests upon the destruction of all impurities.

"But as for the statement that 'the individual soul is liberated through the subtle body,' such [a process] alone is not the subsequent sequence of ascending higher, which follows the order of presiding over locations such as the navel and so forth. (4)
Likewise, because it transcends [the former], it is the higher bondage (uttara-bandha). || 5 ||
Crossing over is the supreme; liberation is the supreme. || 6 ||

Where there are no such superior [arguments], and where that designation of "superior"—namely, the determination that "this is of such a kind" or "that is of such a kind"—does not occur in any way, [that is the case]. ||7||

For this very reason, as long as the illusory subject (māyīya-pramātā) seeks to enter into the unsurpassed form, it remains within the conceptualized (kalpita) alone, characterized by its specific nature. However, that which is inherent therein is the conceptualized form itself, because it flashes forth without [the substrate] being separate; that alone is, in reality, the unsurpassed, and thus belongs to the Supreme Self (parātman).
Where the Śākta, Śāmbhava, and other [means] are not superior, nor are the states of waking and so forth; there, the powers such as Paśyantī and the others are not superior.
And those beginning with Ghorā are the subsequent ones; they do not exist where [the others] are.
And where those [energies] beginning with Parāparā and the others do not exist, that is the North. 11.
And those higher [powers] are all powers where they do not exist.

Likewise, there is no "not" (na) nor "belly" (udara); by that [process], crossing occurs through the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The consciousness of the Guru impels the consciousness of the disciple, but not by means of rituals such as fire-offerings (*homa*) and the like.
Such is this "crossing" (*tara*), which is the act of crossing wherein there is no [need for] self-luminous consciousness that pervades all.
For such a person is devoid of various bases. || 13 ||

Likewise, by the rule *aniti svam iti* [Uṇādi-sūtra 4.519], the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus, the subtle self (*aṇu-ātman*), consisting of the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*) and so forth, is denoted. Furthermore, "breathing" (*ānanam*) refers to life-force (*jīvana*). This is the function known as "living," which resides within the body and other such substrates, being both non-different and different from its powers and so on; it is essentially void-like and is designated as the "void-perceiver" (*śūnya-pramātṛ*). It belongs to that very [self].

Supremacy (*uttaratva*) consists in being superior to all things through the intellect of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dhī*), because [in this state] everything is of the singular nature of Śiva.
For non-inert beings, life is simply their knowledge and action; for inert beings, life is their being the support for that which possesses life. || 14 ||

Likewise, "A" is the first culmination of that [Parā], which consists of the peaceful yet radiant universal reflective awareness (*viśvāmarśana*), the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*) whose nature is non-dual with one's own self— the waveless ocean of consciousness resting in the innate, great light free from artifice (*amāyīya-naisargika-mahāprakāśa*). This [consciousness] resides on the ground of fearlessness.
Thus, it ends with the *visarga*; its "floating" (*plavana*) is its existence as the highest of all, wherein [it resides]. || 15 ||

That in which non-duality and so forth—which do not exist [as separate entities]—are impelled is "anu"; that which is exceedingly *anu* is *anuttara*, because it is non-sequential due to its all-pervasiveness. || 16 ||
Although such a mind has vast meaning, it is summarized for the sake of the disciples' understanding; it is determined in sixteen ways as the unsurpassed (*anuttara*).

For this very reason, it is "unsurpassed" (*niruttara*): either because it is a complete answer (*niḥśeṣeṇa uttaraṃ*), or because it has emerged from what is unsurpassed (*anuttaratvād uttarān nirgatam*), or because it is the answer to all (*sarvair uttaraṃ*), or because it is superior to all (*sarvebhya uttaraṃ*).

And all that, or even more than that, is "prakāśa"—the illuminating nature of graces (vilāsas) or the state of being the illuminator of graces through its own inherent grace. From that, or for that reason, she has "crossed over" it;
she has crossed over it, or she has crossed over it exceedingly (uta uccais tīrṇā). Furthermore, what is she like? For this very reason:

The triad consisting of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu) is the bestower of the poison [of suffering] to that supreme innate vitality (sahajaujas) which is the unity of the triad; for that supreme innate vitality has as its very nature that primordial essence (prakṛti) which is the unity of those three.
If it is argued that since the nature of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul is a triad, how can there be unity therein? [The answer is: Unity exists within that very triad.
If it is argued that unity is impossible, this is true; however, this very triad is itself the unity,
because here the triad of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu) does not denote three separate entities,
but rather refers to a single Supreme Reality which is capable of being described in its various distinct states.

There is no definition of those respective names; rather, Śiva is the previously determined, perfectly complete essence of manifestation (*prathāsāra*). Power (*śakti*) is non-different from Him, and the individual soul (*aṇu*) is the unifier of the two.
Devoid of that unification, he alone receives the various designations such as "living being" (*jīva*) and so forth.

It becomes the vessel for conceptual construction. Through its continuous pursuit, according to the analogy of waves upon water, that very same [consciousness], while being itself, appears as if mounted upon the ignorance it has imagined;
saying "I am not," and so forth, yet through its own self-recognition, it is once again "that very same [consciousness]. Thus, there is no reality whatsoever that is dependent on anything else.

Because that which has every nature as its own nature is a single nature; and if it were not a triad, even oneness would be laughable without the other two. Since even the cognition "one" regarding a single thing is difficult to comprehend, that oneness consisting of the triad is supreme and innate vigor (*ojaḥ*).

"Light" (prakāśa) means its own power or its own strength; by that, it is free from poison, impurity, and defect. "Poison" refers to the ignorance known as saṃsāra, which acts like a venomous serpent; it "shatters" (vi-dārayati), meaning it cuts through or destroys that [ignorance].
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is eternally lofty, distinct from all else, and indestructible.

Non-destruction and supreme joy are its vibration; its emergence is "in this. By this, the immersion (*samāveśa*) of both powers known as Consciousness (*cit*) and Bliss (*ānanda*) is proclaimed in the Supreme (*parā*);
[the immersion] of Will (*icchā*) and Knowledge (*jñāna*) [is proclaimed] in the triad of *paśyantī* and the others to be described hereafter.

Furthermore, what is the nature of the accomplishment of the entry into the ritual actions? That very [nature] is the closing (*nimeṣa*) of the various powers of Maheśvara, which is itself the opening (*unmeṣa*), and the opening is itself the closing; it is the essence of those two, or that by which they exist. It is "opened," meaning blossomed. Furthermore, it is "exceedingly beyond all" (*atīva sarvātītā*).
Transcending all thought, she is the very root of differentiation in such and such ways; she is not false, for she is the primordial subject who,
like a teacher of manifold existence, is the cause of the arts of skill— she who is playful, playful, and full of essence.

O Great Lord of Mantras, O Lord of Mantras, O Primordial of Mantras! You lead [the practitioner] to the stainless seed-syllables of the mantra, which are pure and partless— uttering "hūṃ hūṃ" and so forth, wherein one does not perceive even the differentiated as distinct from one's own self, nor one's own self as something other, as if they were mutually produced by duality.

That Śuddhavidyā, which rests upon the powers of Kalā, Kāla, Rāga, Niyati, and Vala, manifests a state of particularity that, though not mutually contradictory, appears as if it were contradictory; she is skilled in bestowing the state of Vaiśvarī through her radiant splendor. Therefore...
Having made the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) subordinate by means of its expansion beyond the external,
she— while intensely cherishing each and every state, even that which is uncontrolled,
and while rendering the totality of all states fruitless— effects the triadic constitution (*tripuṭīkaraṇa*) consisting of the agent and so forth.

The discerning one, though distinct from the world of qualifiers and qualified such as the "entirety" (*sakala*) and so forth, does not exclude her own internal state of being; rather, by virtue of constantly negating the flow of non-existence, she appears as various— that very reality— just as if she were transcending herself.

Taking up, as it were, another collection of moments characterized by their own distinct definitions, she— possessing the conceit of identifying with the body and so forth— delights at every step through her own forgetfulness; she is adorned with the synthesis of categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and is exceedingly devoted to the systems of logic (*naya*) concerning the unequal, the equal, and both.
Having dissolved their sense of "I" and "mine," as it were, like some [ascetics], the leaders of various religious systems—

through diverse injunctions and prohibitions established by their own descriptions— have made manifest their respective doctrines, which are harsh, direct, and full of difficult-to-comprehend categories of existence.

Manifesting through her auspicious beauty, she is the embodiment of all primordial principles, adorned with the arts of enchantment; she is established in the reality of the earth and other elements, the desired goal, and the sovereign lady who proclaims the supreme lordship of the eminent sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others; she is the effulgence of the great Upanishadic statements, both revealed and concealed.
Skilled in discerning the innate, ultimate essence of the meaning of each respective category,
she manifests exclusively the dullness of the Kāpālika and other doctrines— which rely on powerful illusion, whether straightforward or crooked—
while she herself remains devoid of both the single and the manifold perspectives.

Transcending this state of selfhood, manifesting her own entire, incomparable, and renowned majesty, she is like a peacock’s plumage— vastly spread out, eternal, and possessed of many colors— both here and in the hereafter.

Then, manifesting that very Māyā descended as Mahāmāyā— which was capable of bearing the mass of the most secret contents within that Egg and which revealed from the beginning the path of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas— she appeared.
Measured from the tip of the toe to the crown of the head, she shines with the bliss of non-duality, leaving nothing behind;
she is known through the systems of Yāska and others as being equal toward all six states of existence among all those various conditions, and she is never disregarded by those who have heard her.

The state characterized by the primary notes (*svarādi*) and the like, such as sovereignty (*rājya*) and so forth, does not manifest at all— neither internally nor externally. Speaking as if it were well-prepared and well-accumulated from this and that, it constantly follows the path to dense hell,
illuminating the entire creation of Brahmā (*paitāmaha-sarga*).
Even from the performance of such actions as these, another person—

resplendent with the conceit of being even more subtle than the subtle— ascends further; he is possessed by the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*), and the constant agitation of various thoughts, while his supreme joy dissolves away.
Enveloped by the rags of base desires, born from causes, as if deceived by the inferior [world], deluded by the distractions consisting of food, drink, and the like,
proclaiming wretchedness everywhere, he likewise took refuge in that place of rest.

Addressing great men and eminent personages with such lowly speech as "Victory! and "Live long!", which was improper yet treated as proper, and constantly following after crowds of people like a dog pursuing a bone, he [squandered] his entire paternal inheritance.
Like a house illuminated at creation yet shrouded in darkness and devoid of lamps, he—
his mind wavering and wandering in agitation— having reached the remaining regions, sank somewhere due to being possessed of exceedingly meager strength.

Not knowing that the city of the Self exists outside of the external world, though not small by nature, he makes himself small; and in whom—among the Mahāyānists and others—is he not like one eager for union?
Though ever happy within his own being, he lives in a state of constant lowliness.
Seeking every kind of specialized skill as if his own self were non-self, and being devoted to various desires through extremely harsh asceticism, sacrifice, charity, and so forth,
he became like a lord of some region, performing what was nearly exhausted, and thus became the ruler of another heaven.
Having attained the fallen woman who has made the quarters her sacrificial creeper through conquest,

I— who am the performer of various ritual preparations— am capable of sporting in the Nanda garden or of captivating the mind of the Apsaras with the thunderbolt-weapon, for my supreme glory shines forth eternally.
I am the supporter of the universe, yet I am nowhere; I am everywhere, for I transcend all.

This entire universe manifests as my family, and I alone appear in such various ways throughout the whole world. By my own power, the universe vibrates; no power is experienced by anyone other than me.

"I am the one skilled in all arts; from me alone comes the birth of this universe, and its maintenance and dissolution are likewise always firmly established in me. Having thus contemplated within myself that my great power is spread everywhere, I remain indifferent in some places, and in others, I abide within my own self."

Having assumed the nature of fire, I am celebrated by that Śrī as the one who, through the offering of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and other rites, satiates delusion; as the giver of the arising of various movements and as the foremost among the hosts of gods, I alone am renowned. At every opportune moment, they offer oblations into me.
Having cast fear far away, they took refuge in him who sits in tranquility; and so it was that all the flames, though ever-towering at their extremities, remained here in this very world.

Abiding in a state of constant overflowing splendor, he—though appearing as a mere fragment—triumphs over me, for he is endowed with the power of the essence of the arts. Thus he reflected within himself.

And in some places, having projected the state of Dharmarāja (the King of Dharma) upon his own self, he was consecrated in bringing about the equalization of both the equal and the unequal among people; perceiving the past, the future,
and the present states of all beings, even those hidden within the body-cottages of wandering ascetics.
Bestowing fear and attachment upon people, he makes their existence flicker like blades of grass; at every step, he reckons the time of all and the non-time.
As if by deception, he causes the moving and the unmoving to fall into disorder on all sides, while his own command is ordained over them.

Repeatedly, from end to beginning, how is it that this poorly understood [reality], though somehow attained and remaining for even an eon, leads only to dissolution— its qualities becoming attenuated; alas,
in all its various manifestations, it causes itself to vanish as if it were something far better!
By that human exertion, he proclaims his own power to the host of gods; with the syllable *huṃ*,
he renders the arrogant host tranquil and devoid of splendor, like one possessing supreme sovereignty and vast vigor over the entire assembly.

Thinking, "I alone am capable of commanding the people as if they were female slaves; there is no other like me," and conceiving the notion, "I alone am the Supreme Lord of the worlds and the Destroyer," he distinguishes himself by his own arrogance, like one whose splendor is enhanced by the fullness of all his gathered power and wealth.
And in some places, displaying his own majesty first while abasing his pride through that sovereignty over the lords of demons which was thus undistinguished from theirs,
he made each class of immortals appear like a mere leaf upon a tree, their splendor eclipsed by his world-transcending luster.

Free from heaviness like the wind, constantly bringing about lightness, the Goddess Śrī— endowed with vast wealth and dancing with the playful charms of manifold illusions— scatters [her devotees] here and there; yet among all those, even a single one, by virtue of his immense strength, begins to manifest her own bewilderment.
Having personally subdued Kālāmā and made him the lord of that very house,
and having brought this multitude of people under his own control by performing penance that surpassed the commands of Brahmā and the other gods,
you shine forth in various ways, victorious and free from all fear of others.

I am one who has attained supreme vigor and the excellence of all remaining arts; I have purified my lineage and am adorned with the entirety of royal splendor shining upon the highest station; I am someone endowed with every fruit in its completeness, long-lived, and sought after even by young women.

Possessing ever-arisen youth, he alone, assuming many forms, conceives the self-conceit, "I conquer. And in some places, having projected within himself by his own self the state of being the Lord of All Waters,
he is renowned for his pure fame due to his mastery over the discipline of various appropriate groups of beings.

Victorious is the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśāna), who, though his splendor is exceedingly diminished, surpasses the waters of rivers, oceans, and the like; for he adorns his own body with his own limbs— which possess variegated lusters through various colors— manifested by water, like a multitude of gems, in a manner that is truly wondrous.

Though he has cast far away the pride of the lowly, this lord of rivers possesses the majesty of his own innate power; with the beautiful banner of the great fish surging aloft, may this teacher of the wise,
remaining for a long time, experience his own state somewhere.
And by some such illusion as this, oh, this very form has been assumed— the one whose nature is darkness, who shines within all, known as Prāṇa, who,
through the increasing delusion of his own power, is the cause of the movement of the entire world and the witness of all that exists.

The purifier of all that purifies, capable of inflaming the fire and arranging even a crumbling mountain into many stable forms; though consuming everything, he is the cause of its nourishment; skilled in performing the fivefold actions, he is divided into tenfold aspects and shines with intense brilliance.
And he whose own state is always moving, who is exceedingly prosperous everywhere,

spreading his plumage like a cluster of bees among the trees with various movements, driving about even living beings that have not yet been born here and there, distinguishes himself; and for what purpose does he not [distinguish] himself anywhere?

And he was not one who indulged in luxuries, yet he was highly esteemed by the great; he was Mahādeva, who considered himself the sovereign of kings, though his majesty was fashioned from delusion; he was Kuvera, whose crown was adorned by the radiance of various meritorious beings, and whose lotus-hand shone with the splendor of all prosperities and the nine treasures.
The Lord of the others, borne by men, shining even more intensely than Amarāvatī,
the lord of light, was being celebrated with loud-sounding *kāhalī* and *muraja* drums by the *kiṃpuruṣas* and hosts of *gandharvas* in the city of Alakā.
Victorious is he who, being led to delight by hosts of celestial nymphs joined together with those ascended to higher realms— through enchanting song, instrumental music, and dance—
and who delights in various pastimes here and there in the Caitraratha grove and the special regions of Rāmasthala, as well as in the city of Alakā.

O Īśāna, having yourself accepted [the sovereignty], you have, by the power of your own innate and distinguished majesty and resolve, brought under your control the entire host of gods; eternally radiant,
you are skilled in perceiving the playful charms of Satī residing within your own limbs, for the sake of others and yet beyond others.

The one who is worshipped by lords, who has transcended hundreds of calculations, who is the source of the entire universe, who has utterly conquered the agitation of the delusive passion that bewilders all minds, who knows from his own nature the beginning and end of everything, the conqueror of death, meditated upon as "Om."

The Lord of the ten great siddhis, such as *rucira*, *cirasthāyin*, and *pada-icchā*, the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) who is proclaimed by names such as Hara and others that are not false, is necessarily being carried away by the host of deities headed by Gaṇeśa; he has transcended the supreme counting of all beings.
By virtue of being the Supreme, he is devoted to that [Supreme]; as the Bull-vehicled One (*Vṛṣavāha*), he is the one who possesses the Bull.

Thus, even for those who possess extensive contradictions—such as the dualities of the sacrificial priests (*ṛtvij*)—he is a wondrous magician who brings them together in a single assembly, by means of his state as the Supreme Lord who transcends all duality in an instant.
He whose power is renowned, who is both existence and non-existence, the bestower of absolute fearlessness to all, the Lord of Gaurī, who establishes a multitude of various tantras,
who transforms even the great poison into the state of supreme nectar, and whose pair of feet are worshipped by gods and asuras— he shines forth with valor.

And where else could he— possessing a pair of lotus feet resplendent with the brilliance of emerald stones, having assumed the state of the Grandfather (Brahmā) due to being deeply rooted in supreme illusion, and being worthy of universal homage because his majesty is fully known— be found?
Exercising supreme reverence, ever established in the state of being the speaker of hundreds of words,
skilled in manifesting such and such diverse multitudes of creations, and by nature possessing a firm abiding in the state of supreme peace, he is the author of the four Vedas through his action.

He is the external supreme bridge, a clever wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) skilled in manifold arts; he is intent upon granting boons through the splendor of various divine powers, the bestower of fearlessness for all that is thought of, and the giver of the bondage of ritual injunctions, prohibitions, and other actions— even to Nārāyaṇa himself, in his various fish-incarnations.

He is capable of performing the descent into the maṭhas and yonis and of issuing commands; he is the instructor who simultaneously teaches what is beneficial and what is harmful, as well as what is to be adopted and what is to be avoided; he is skilled in the contemplation of various kalpas and their conclusions, and in the investigation of the samayas; he is proficient in the supreme method that is consistent with reality and free from falsehood; and he is one in whom all [qualities] are firmly established.

May the elephant-faced Lord always triumph—he who is ever full of joy, yet whose hope is fulfilled; who, having become a mouse-vehicle in some places, is skilled and struck down by many obstacles; whose single tusk is as bright as the autumnal moon;
and who, through his union with Puṣṭi, is constantly turned away from worldly existence while facing toward the sacrifice.

First, he is honored as the Lord of the Gate (Dvāreśa); renowned as the bestower of boons (Varada) and the beloved son of Bhavānī even more than Kārtikeya; skilled in sporting within the waters of the exceedingly pure Payasvati river; and manifesting supreme power toward his devotees without any display of ferocity.

In the presence of those various groups of attendants headed by Nandin, the Three-eyed Lord— delighted by their manifold activities and his own supreme devotion, and having obtained diverse enjoyments—
indulges himself with many playful arts; for it is this very Māyā of his that acts thus somewhere.
The Lord of the Eight Devas, having become self-controlled and free from pride, though possessing the conceit of birth in various places such as the realms of gods and others,
sports with a joyful nature even among the wombs of Daityas and the like.

Having fixed his soul upon himself and abandoned his own most peaceful nature, that arrogant man displays harsh behavior and terrifies the gods and others; having attained the state of the sun at some point through his own powerful and playful sports—
Worthy of praise by all, the king of kings over many hosts of stars and hosts of planets,
the primary witness of all actions among every undertaking,
the supreme cause for the direct perception of various states of being, he is difficult to overcome.
Renowned for his power in slaying and seizing Death, even as he rolls upon the great path of the sky which is without support,

the Sun— possessing feet more harsh than a lion’s— bears the names Sūrya, Pūṣan, and others, in order to experience here itself the divine state of immortality that was destroyed by the mere remembrance of his exceedingly cruel feet.

Sometimes this lord of birds [Garuda] appears as a malevolent spirit, and even the moon, though a mass of fame, is like the mouth of Brahma’s cosmic egg; yet the very one who adorns the crest of the Lord whose crown is graced by the moon with his many digits, and who is the life-giver to the beloved of Rati, becomes the cause of danger to the lives of women separated from their lovers— truly, everything is such.
Delighting people with the moonlight of his own reasoning, and being the cause of the thirst for [his] poetry,
this very [author], whose great fame is celebrated for his friendship toward the night-lotus, causes the quarters of the sky to blossom; furthermore,
he alone is capable of accomplishing that which is otherwise difficult to achieve.

Consisting of delusion, characterized by the non-existence of that which is unreal, and utterly devoid of consciousness— though its own multitude of powers has been completely subdued and contracted by Māyā— it remains bound by limitation; clinging to those very states of existence, it persists.
Manifesting Himself in various forms within the beautiful abodes of Surabhi and others,
He is renowned as the "Cow of Plenty" and so forth; indeed, having become all things,
He alone shines thus in every place— both now and in the future— as this very same singular Self through His own supreme grace toward others.
Having been awakened by the Lord,

with a mind distressed by the entirety of *saṃsāra*, seeking the investigation of his own Self, he performs the performance of obligatory and occasional rites, worship, and expiation, while avoiding what is prohibited and performing what is enjoined according to the rules.
With his entire impurity removed through disciplined practice, his mind exceedingly pure and radiant,
and his senses exhausted by the act of offering himself as a sacrifice,
he— possessing the wealth of the means such as tranquility and self-restraint— questions his very own Self, the Teacher.

And the true guru, having beheld Suśīla with a most cooling gaze and having reflected upon him, rescued him— like one submerged in turbulent water— from his lack of discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things, and established him in his own Lord, the Self, which is ever-risen and firmly rooted.

Having dispelled fear and being filled with the essence of bliss, she reveals a state where the perilous narrowness of base pride has dissolved; by means of the gradual ascent of the ladder, she first makes manifest the stages beginning with Lokāyata, and then, having fully integrated them, she brings about the supreme repose.

He causes [the soul] to ascend to the ground, and at the end, having praised that Supreme Person as his own dear Lord, he himself reflects upon his own self, thinking: "My own self is this body composed of the five elements; it is the cause of the joy and aesthetic delight of my own limbs, which are beautiful with their various parts."

In this incomplete state, O Haṃsakalā, I am incomplete; yet when all the powers of consciousness are present, I become whole. Just as the digit of bliss is perceived when [the elements] are combined, so too this consciousness of the elements does not exist when they are separate.

Furthermore, that which is worthy of being seen is perceived by those who have gathered together as something not to be carried away, like the wrinkles of old age upon me; yet again, it is not seen at all by them when they are divided, due to their state of partiality,
for indeed, when they are divided, there is nothing at all.

Disregarding the doctrine of the Cārvākas, while remaining right here and not obtaining even a fraction of his own bliss, he experiences the subsequent dearness of the senses as the showers of the rain of weapons fall upon him.
Because one experiences the closing of the eyes upon hearing harsh words,
the contraction of the ears upon smelling a foul odor, the shrinking of the nose even when encountering an unpleasant touch, or the withdrawal of the tongue from a beloved object.
Indeed, it is not at all possible for one who has endured the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*)— which perform dear deeds—
to [remain indifferent] toward that nature (*nisarga*) described in the scriptures as "in which all is, from whence all is," and so forth; for through the experience of these very [organs],
they serve as the instruments for various enjoyments and the like, just as a blind person [relies on others].

And because one perceives a greater degree of dearness in the physical body than in those [other elements], one conceives that their very nature is unstable; thus, no longer experiencing one's own supreme bliss even there, one thinks: "I am not the senses, but I am the vital breath (prāṇa) intensified by them."
For by this alone [the penis], even though dry, thirst is quenched; in the absence of these two, there is the destruction of the body and so forth.
Among the various elemental constituents (*bhūtakalā*), this [penis] alone is capable of assuming a fivefold or tenfold form of the body, whereas the other is not.
No one here possesses such power; and even for those such as the deaf and the mute, because their very life-breath is desirous of this [bliss], it is found to be beloved above all else.
Following that sequence, having reflected, "This alone is my own self," there occurs a succession of delusions arising from the failure to attain supreme joy even therein.
Beyond even that, the mind calculates: "This is not my self, nor is this my own life-force; rather, whatever it conceives and discriminates as ever-new appearances of existence leads to violence."
The Purāṇa is like a stone compared to the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, that which has been established in the *Aṇu* [Yoga] is also nothing but the mind of expanded power (*vitataujomanas*).

Whether it moves continuously internally or externally, whether it is intoxicated by its own nature through eternity, or even having entered into the realization "I am that very [Brahman]," one must experience it as such.

Because there is no attainment of bliss through the mere ascent upon the paths, he becomes even more anxious and investigates a further development: that the very nature of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is of the form of certainty—is the cause of knowledge for the mind (*manas*) as well as for itself;
for in its absence, the mind and the other faculties remain in a state of flux.
Upon ascending to that experience, because of the state of being established in the knowledge of That, one feels, "Only this [Self] ought to be my own Self," as if taking a moment's rest;
yet, even while constantly [engaged], due to the lack of the play of innate discrimination, there is the bliss of one's own experience.
Not finding even that [state], he discerns it as being supreme, yet thinks: "This too is not my Self.

Indeed, when the path of experience—consisting of the notion "I am the body" due to the persistence of ignorance within knowledge—is ascended for even a moment, one regards that very ignorance as one's own eternal Self.

Having conceptualized [this], he causes his own self to rest for a moment even beyond that— in the doctrines of momentary consciousness, external objects, emptiness, the self, and so forth— by being intent on the investigation of appearances, yet without dissolving even there due to the persistence of conceptualization.

Having become even more intent on the distinction between self and other, with one's inner faculties rendered dysfunctional by improper reflection, how can one who is utterly incapable of resolute effort resolve that "I am momentary consciousness," given that therein the formative forces (saṃskāras) arise as a mere semblance of existence?

Otherwise, due to the absence of the capacity to connect one thing with another at one time and another thing at another time, all worldly transaction would be uprooted; consequently, the entire world would either become as if mute or, even in the case of the theory of sentence-meaning (*vākyārthavāda*), it would always remain [confined] to individual word-meanings (*padārtha*).

Since deep sleep, dreaming, and illusion would necessarily cease to exist due to being fixed in pure knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhatva*), or because it is impossible for one's own self to be the sustainer of the universe if one were to contemplate its non-existence; and since this [universe] is like a dream or a waking state, how could it be either a cause or an independent entity? In the first case, never at any time...
Its state of being obscured by ignorance is untenable, because an independent [self] does not admit of being subject to suffering;
or, even if that were admitted, no cause for it could be found. Furthermore, in the second case [if it were dependent], it would be possible for others—whether visible or invisible—to [be the cause].
Because they do not attain the state of the Supreme Lord, and because even they conceive of themselves as eternal by virtue of all [attributes],

therefore, in either case, agency is not appropriate for them; nor, then, could there be enjoyership, for in the state of being an enjoyer, there would necessarily follow the consequence of constant enjoyment, which contradicts their very nature of purity.

Because it would entail the consequence of the impossibility of liberation due to the nature of existence being eternal; because it would result in the futility of the various doctrines investigated by many philosophical systems; because it would lead to the pursuit of another body for everyone at all times; and because, since light would never arise, there would be an absolute lack of finality—therefore, [liberation] does not exist in the state of being an enjoyer.

If the self is about to undergo a consecration (abhiṣeka), yet there is some other person here who is non-insentient (jaḍa) but authorized by the ancients, what kind of discernment is there for that non-insentient being— whether the cause is accepted as it appears to itself, or when the cause is not obtained?

Because that [object] is grasped by those very [senses], it is possible for there to be error, since the innate [nature] itself, through its inability to distinguish between itself and another, produces the appearance of both self and other;
furthermore, if this [cognition] possesses desire, how could it not be insentient? And if it does not perceive, how then [could it see]?

If it is argued that the object of perception might sometimes be insentient and sometimes sentient, then those who hold such views are themselves deluded in many ways; how could they inform others of their own similar delusions? Therefore, it is better that a dispute be regarded as having no basis for investigation at all.
Enough with that [distinction]; for some, through the display of their own novel and diverse intellects,
have fallen into the state of being Pātañjala by means of arguments consisting of the frantic activity of delusion— [arguments] which are neither ancient nor even new.

In that [system] as well, the Self (ātman) is established as being untouched by afflictions (kleśa), karma, and the locus of their maturation (vipākāśaya); it is itself eternally existent, distinct from the transmigrating being, and ever-free from defects or taints; and it is the instrument for various cognitions by virtue of being reflected within the primary constituent (pradhāna) and its sattva-quality.

It is certainly not appropriate for them either to show such great respect, since they themselves have pointed out the defects of their own system; for if this [system] is held in such high regard by them, then it must be the work of some particular person who has already removed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and other obstacles, and who is a supreme being (*satva*).

Since that reflection functions as an object precisely by virtue of being a reflection, it is not distinct from it; for all things, because they are always desired in every worldly transaction, it is the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, which are constantly manifesting, that always constitute the world and the like through their heroic nature, and thus it does not exist as something different from them.
Such a view, which is obstructed from the state of supreme bliss by its own inherent nature and its various fixed,

self-imposed constraints, is indeed a delusion; for even that [view] is presented as being free from error by those who have been captivated by the play of their own imagination, yet it is actually established through the perspective of the Jains regarding the categories of the living (jīva), the non-living (ajīva), and so forth.

Among the nine categories of objects, one who has abandoned all that is to be discarded, who has removed the multitude of ten defects, whose bonds of karma have dissolved through the removal of worldly enjoyments, who is patient with the pairs of opposites,
and who is free from pride regarding caste and other such distinctions— such a person, like the Arhat himself, is accepted as one's own self.

Nor is this [objection] valid; for even though it is devoid of defects and distinct from this or that [object], the Self cannot abandon its indifference toward every enjoyment— whether it be constant, pervasive, guarded, traversed, or even renounced—
because the seed of that [enjoyment] remains inevitably present in the mind, whether it has passed away or been destroyed here by someone.
Whether it remains eternally new or at some point becomes something else through its association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is the Lord who manifests as such;
therefore, those statements of theirs are indeed to be rejected because they lack true intent, for by clinging to them, not even a trace of bliss is produced. Now, regarding the body...
He who is overflowing with the agitation of the senses, yet whose movement is always easily attained by virtue of being the cause of the digit of knowledge;
he who is identical with that state and its measure,
who is the essence of all, and who eternally shines everywhere— he alone is this one's own Self.
Even in that path consisting of the vision of the sky-clad (the Jains), alas, there is no hope for me to obtain the surge of wealth, since such a self— though being struck down—
would necessarily arise by its own nature through the conceptualization of forms, however subtle it may be considered by them.
In whatever way that state of being is freed from conceptualization, even its formless nature is indeed worthy of veneration;

when venerated in such a manner, one may even fall into the mire of passion, hatred, loathing, and so forth. Thereafter, through the dissolution of joy, one becomes truly immersed in the infinite, as if having attained that very state.

Thinking that human effort would be supreme, they have not even conceived the idea of taking up this [path], for here there is no possibility of attaining even a fraction of liberation; moreover, beyond this, Śrī Vāsudeva is the primordial nature, while other individual souls (jīvas) are like the embers produced from Him, as if from fire.

If this Jina, even while abiding by the Pāñcarātra system, were capable of continuously and incessantly manifesting these [qualities] through the swallowing-up of their origination— possessing power even in their suppression precisely because of that very capacity— then he would not be distinguished from others by his joy.
Because that [world] is composed of the very collection of those various external riches,
and because it is burdened by the weight of conceiving diverse pairs of opposites, it is— whether upon investigation or otherwise—
incapable of transcending its absorption in that [collection], even though it is distinct from it; and immediately thereafter...

Known according to the Pāśupata doctrine, [the Lord] is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), and He alone is to be worshipped; the relationship between cause and effect is the means of reviving [the soul], and by destroying the bonds of the bound (paśu-pāśa),
He is the cause of generating specific liberation, yet He does not attain the nature of the self while appearing [as such].

Since even one's own light is subject to effort and non-effort through the powerful process of cause and effect in living, the bond of the individual soul within bodies is released by the utterance of *praṇava*; yet, even that is difficult to ward off. If it is not warded off, then existence cannot be removed from being; thus, this worldly existence persists within being.

Even though the individual soul (jīva) worships that [deity] of existence, it is not empowered to attain the state of liberation; for even this doctrine, though practiced by them, is loathsome because it leads to the attainment of [rebirth],
and its extensive praise is like a stream of nectar poured into a vessel other than one's own, which is quickly consumed by the demons of passion.

Even by the science of grammar (*śabdaśāsana*), which possesses doubt and purpose, that which is investigated from the perspective of word and meaning— the innate nature of all things, which functions as the basis for all worldly transactions— is revealed; though stainless, it is manifested through the form of *sphoṭa* at the beginning and at the end.

Even here, the view that "the Self is indeed Śabdabrahman with its adjuncts (sāñjanaḥ)" does not at all find favor among the wise; for even here, the existence [of the Self] culminates in a repose within its own nature, since the notion of "I" regarding this limit (idaṃtā) is merely figurative, as the word itself [is reduced to its essence].
