Because an object is insentient by nature and dependent upon that [knowledge], and because even if it were independent, it would be incapable of grasping its own meaning without a knower— indeed, neither the word nor the object is able to know its own meaning by itself apart from a knower; such is this [situation].
Even the mere appearance of those who know the science of grammar is illusory; therefore, one should be a conqueror of this [illusion] through its abiding state.

Yet, for one who is attached to the bondage of karma and possesses a fierce form, there is no interval even from passion. Furthermore, I am not at all that "Puruṣa" who is renowned as a follower of the doctrine of Kapila; I am nothing whatsoever.
Furthermore, because the Puruṣa established by that [system] is incapable of agency without Prakṛti,

and because Prakṛti itself is essentially insentient, their doctrine of reflection (pratibimbavāda) is likewise ineffective; for what is merely a reflected appearance is not like the original object (bimba) in any way.
Even though the state of being a laborer is mixed [with other qualities],

it is experienced as such because only the reflection of light appears in the mirror and so forth, and not its heat; therefore, for these [reflections] as well, [the distinction] is in every respect...
In this very state, one should remain indifferent, for by abiding here, one experiences liberation from all things. Having thus transcended everything through the teaching of the Upaniṣads,
O Arjuna, one realizes one's own Self as being devoid of arising and destruction, with all particular defects pacified.

May that which is the remainder of all, in which every self-conceived affliction has dissolved, which is more supreme than the supreme, as pure as the highest ether, the cause of enmity toward this entire world, the resting place for those of wicked pride and intellect—
may it lead one along the path of supreme discernment, just as anyone [might lead another].

In the supreme bliss, the innate, one's own, true, eternal, pure, and free from the appearance of duality; in that awakened state which is everywhere, in every way, at all times, and in all places; in the powerful field of consciousness (*vittala*) which swallows both existence and non-existence; in that state devoid of the movement of all impurities and parts—by means of that [state], may the primordial "I-ness" (*rādyahantā*) arise.
It is free from error, devoid of both the conditioned and the unconditioned, and divested of the cultivation of objective existence;

though it is renowned as the blazing fire within the dense thicket of great delusion for all beings, it remains inexpressible, as if concealed by ignorance, yet its excellent nature shines forth at every step, as established by the Upaniṣads.
It is fitting that I become that very Supreme Self,
for it has been directly realized here through the time of my own true experience; thus,
let this very place be my own garden, the abode of rest from the great confusion of delusion.

O Marha, it is for this very purpose that the fruitfulness of the entire cultivation of means, headed by the pacification of all states, is realized; and this alone is the supreme reality of Brahman, which the sages have determined to be beyond all categories and as "That" (Sat) in the supreme scriptures. Therefore, it is so.

This very supreme secret consciousness, which brings about the experience of non-dual Brahman, shines forth as the radiance of the arising of supreme bliss; by means of this alone, great beings— whose connection to bondage and its persistence has been severed— behold Maheśvara as Om.

Those whose movements have reached the clarity of the supreme state shine forth; they alone, through the experience of existence after existence, manifest most intensely as the power of dissolution. Even though these two—the non-dual Śiva and the Great Non-dual (Mahādvaya)—shine forth as superior, nevertheless, they do not transcend that [supreme state]; for she is liberated even from those two.
In the non-dual system of Śiva, the very manifestation of the glory of one's own experience is sufficient;

here, the doctrine of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-vāda*) alone prevails, which constructs the state of being both causeless and causal, dispelling the darkness of ignorance again and again, and wherein the performance of the fivefold cosmic acts is essentially nothing other than one's own self-reflection.
The distinguished Great Non-duality, the supreme refuge and unsurpassed experience of the secret,

must manifest by itself through passion alone; in every way, even that very thing is most proximate here through the path of non-dual supreme bliss, and thus it is exactly as it is from this and that, and beyond.
When Hari has been perceived in the mountain peaks and other such places, when mental constructs have dissolved, and when baseless desires have become attenuated,

then at one time those various specific regions— more delightful than the delight itself, bestowing the nectar of non-duality, and consisting of supreme bliss— are indeed perceived. O Lord, such is the playful dance of Your manifestation.
Having ascertained through scripture and other means that this very Self of the Upaniṣads—

the supreme non-dual whose nature is undivided— is indeed characterized by the sixfold marks according to its specific residual manifestations in various regions like Śiva and others, there arises a manifest conviction.

For the purpose of removing erroneous conceptions, one should first engage in the threefold method consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*)— which is established through various authentic scriptures according to the distinctions imagined therein— and then, having withdrawn from worldly activity for the sake of instruction, one should practice with right speech and truthfulness.
Having tasted her own state through her own essence until the limit of generating direct realization,
she herself reveals her own experienced condition— that which has become the object of the playful manifestation of her own bliss,
which bestows grace upon others, and which has deceived all defilements.
With the root of the conceit of "I" regarding one's own life-span dissolved, and with all difficult contractions vanished, may [the state] be entirely universal,
free from dwarfing pride, unprecedented, ever-present, and devoid of priority or posteriority.

The great subduer of all false views, the essence of essences, the destroyer of the wandering through saṃsāra, skillful in the withdrawal of those rushing toward calamity, possessing a vast and exalted joy that is the supreme flavor, whose neighing renders the thirst for sense objects in vain, and who proclaims the well-spoken truth— [I bow] to the Ascetic.

May [He]—whose radiant splendor is ever-new and scorching; whose excellence dispels the accumulated karma that causes false fear; who brings about the crushing torment of hell and other realms for those of wicked and inferior intellect; who is eternally serene and never at any time diminished—[grant his grace].
It is entirely present, unobstructed, uncreated, incomparable, transcending time, the most excellent vision, unsurpassed,
without interval, continuous, free from the fear of the arising of dissolution, eternally risen, and its own intrinsic clarity.

That which is non-deceptive, beyond the locus of speech, free from the impulsion of injunctions and prohibitions, exceedingly pleasing to the heart, faultless, inexhaustible, having destroyed all that is to be destroyed,
not proceeding [as a conditioned flow], yet existing as the past, present, and future, and eternally abiding.
Existing as the equality of all that is equal, this very nature of mine—which is formless, yet the sole measure of innate self-experience—is the form to be contemplated.
"Aho! I am Brahman; I am He; I am That; I am all; I am the Self of all; there is no 'mine'."

I am that very one who, being alone and desiring nothing else, manifests all this for my own sport out of my innate and natural power, and thus become such as I am, in accordance with the various karmas imagined by myself.

Thus, for this very [Self], even though it is partless (*niraṃśa*), its self-luminosity shines forth intensely; therein, presided over by pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), whether as one or many, the "this-ness" (*idantā*) does not manifest at all.

The meaning of the verbal root [in *sākṣin*] is established as "that which is not touched by parts in any way whatsoever," by means of that [consciousness] which has dispelled the light of manifestation (*vivarta-tejas*) because it does not depend on any objective state (*bhāva*). Thus, the first part, consisting of knowledge that is dissolving away through fragmentation, is designated as the "Witness" (*sākṣin*). From that...

Presiding over the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), distinguished by attributes such as omniscience and the like, possessing a renowned, vast, and uncreated great power, the universal vibration, the one worthy of salutation,
whose bliss is the gentle home of his own divine play.
The Supreme Lord is thus distinguished; according to the gradual calculation of the power and manifestation of the elements,
He alone— though of a single nature— is bound by the knot of knots through a threefold self as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and [Śiva].

Manifested there in the form of Maheśvara, he who possesses the conceit of being the creator is called Brahmā, the Lord of the Earth, the Self-born, and the Master of the World; he is celebrated in the Āgamas as one whose nature consists of the play of the power of the manifested universe, and beyond him is the Supreme.
Viṣṇu, whose greatness is known through being the object of the conceit of those who regard him as their protector, who is capable of bestowing grace upon his devotees,
and who is the Lord of Śrī, is proclaimed as such; he whose expansion of power through various incarnations has rescued the multitude of the pride of the foremost among the Asuras.
He who has turned back from the ocean of great calamities that are difficult for even the best of gods to restrain;
who, through his nature as the destroyer, possesses the rising pride of being beyond all else; the lord of Śrī Pārvatī’s life-breath;
the traveler on the singular Great Path; he whose wandering is free from the agitation of desire.

Because he sequentially wards off both [extremes] and is called the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya) and so forth, he is celebrated everywhere as Maheśvara— the one who establishes the auspiciousness of the Supreme Lord, the possessor of being,
who is the essence of all beings, and who is Viṣṇu, the dispeller of darkness.

And Maheśvara is possessed of delusion; therein, ignorance is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) that serves as the cause, and Īśvara is precisely that [Self] qualified by that adjunct. Thus, for this very Īśvara, there arise the four-faced, four-armed, five-faced, and other forms.

Male forms such as Bhāratī, Lakṣmī, Bhavānī, and others, as well as female forms, and even other incarnations such as Matsya and Kūrma, manifest through divine play for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees; furthermore, the third aspect consists of the instruments of reasoning and their mental impressions (*saṃskāras*).

The one called the *jīva*, conditioned by knowledge and delimited by externality, is taught; though the *jīva* is also of a single essential nature, it is proclaimed to be threefold. Thus, due to its association with the elements (*tatojaskatayā*), it is described as follows: therein, the state of waking consists of the identification with the body, which is delimited by the locus of the organs of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, when one is devoid of the conceit of the gross body and is endowed with two adjuncts (*upādhi*),
being possessed of the conceit of the dream-body, one is called *taijasa*. Within the prison of the body, as it were, various well-known and established delusions arise, as if from within.

Just as the sprout and so forth reside within the seed, the universe resides within Me; it attains growth through time and undergoes decay here. Even in this growth and decay, I alone am the temporal agent;
I alone am the supreme connoisseur of its relishing; and I alone am the body and all else.

Just as even without the multitude of supreme bliss, one is capable of performing the functions of knowledge and action regarding the body and so forth— as in a dream— whereby I sport with the restless desire for various diversions by manifesting both similar and dissimilar states through my own great illusion (*mahāmāyā*); so too do I act.
Manifesting my own states within myself alone, as if manifold, I sport; having become a living soul and encountered the vast, dense, and beautiful process pervading the universe,
I wander through various places in such and such ways, deluded.

O noble one, repeatedly accomplishing all my tasks without exception, clothed in the garment of my own sublime power and filled with supreme joy, whom— whom among the infinite states of being— do I not manifest myself, like a mirror, as the self-perfected Great Lord? Somewhere, I am indeed that.
Sometimes possessing a gentle form, and sometimes a fierce form, even without the operation of the senses,

I am renowned as the one fit to perform various actions; thus, O wise one, I take refuge in my own powers and have established my greatness, my pervasiveness being such that it is not transgressed, just as [the serpent's power] exists within its own body.
Just as there is no hearing without the ear, yet the act of hearing occurs in that very place;

just as there is no walking without feet, yet the movement of walking occurs in the body; just as there is no grasping without a hand, yet the sequence of hand-movements occurs in the body; just as there is no writing without speech, yet the composition of a book occurs in the body; and just as there is no crying without a child, yet the act of crying occurs in the body.
Laughter without a cause for laughter, such as the laughter on the body of Mahendra;

the function of a single eye despite possessing thousands of eyes, like the fame of those who are exceedingly harsh; the conception of an embryo by female cranes through the sound of thunderclouds without the pleasure of sexual union—such are these things.
Even in the darkness of one's own body during the night,
he who is free from the conceit of the senses, having integrated this agency— which arises through the instruments [of perception]—
as a mere state of being that is to be contemplated and which transcends thought-constructs (nirvikalpa), becomes a unifier.

That very *prājña* who rests solely within his own ignorance is explained here; although he is one due to the absence of distinctions in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) because of his identification with the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), an internal distinction is nevertheless designated for him. The Witness (*sākṣin*), however, is the synthesizer of all.

Pervading all, known as the Fourth (turya), supremely pure, innate, and natural, it is always and everywhere of one single kind; therein, even through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), there is nowhere any division, for it is not subject to contempt.
Since even those adjuncts are themselves by nature of a single essence, this alone [is the truth].

In the Vedāntic tradition, the Lord who is the witness is described as the subject (dṛk-padārtha) by virtue of His being the living self (jīvatayā). Furthermore, the other—the world-phenomenon (prapañca), consisting of ignorance, its pervasion, and its effects—is, though non-different from Him, like something distinct for the sake of His own divine play; this is the object of perception (dṛśya-padārtha).

Thus it has been declared; even though that [world] is ultimately real, its nature as a worldly delusion—manifested by itself and arising from the union of the power of supreme bliss—is indicated here. Its existence is accepted [in this sense], yet it is not useless like the objects of a dream.

Because it is useful for its worship and so forth, that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which is explained as being of the nature of an object of perception, is also threefold, distinguished as the manifest (*vyākṛta*) and the unmanifest (*mūrta* and *amūrta*). Among these, that "light" (*bhāsā*)— which is the power (*śakti*) that is the seed of the manifold world (*prapañca*) of the manifest and unmanifest— is not produced by that [light], yet it is removed by it.
O King, although it is difficult to turn back, because it does indeed turn back, that consciousness which pervades it—

along with the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) arising from their connection, and the appearances of consciousness (cidābhāsa)— is called "unmanifest" (avyākṛta) due to its beginninglessness and its having attained existence through these [appearances]. Furthermore, the forms of the manifest and unmanifest (mūrtāmūrta) are merely the auxiliary aspects of this very [consciousness].
Though itself insentient, [the intellect] is illumined by the non-insentient reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*);

impelled by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous lives and the karma of the individual soul (*jīva*), it takes as its objects the fivefold objects of knowledge— sound and so forth— and the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) corresponding in number to those objects.
And that ignorance produces those various past and non-past elemental qualities,
which are strung one after another like beads upon the thread of the successive elemental qualities.
That very ignorance which prevents [the light] from entering is itself dependent on that [object]; thus, darkness also is indeed a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) consisting of concealment, which,
being produced by the eye, assumes a state opposed to visual cognition and is removable by light.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the system of the Upaniṣads (*nigamānta-mata*) is that [the Self], like a great flame and so forth, appears and then disappears;

for it is taught in the context of creation by the Śruti and other texts that it is not [the cause of transmigratory existence], since it takes on various specific bodies as its limiting adjuncts (*upādāna*). This is the limit of time (*kāla-kāṣṭhā*).
Furthermore, because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no further arousal of the prior ignorance;

rather, the subsequent [ignorance] is indeed included within the void. And that very thing which is the indeterminate category (*avyākṛta-padārtha*), known as the power (*śakti*) or seed (*bīja*) of the syllable *Om*, is established as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord (*Īśvara*) through its proximity to unity. These are they.
And the subtle, formless five elements— space, air, and so forth—
when united as a single cause within the mobile [Prakṛti] which is situated beyond the Will (icchā) and pervaded by the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-śakti* and *kriyā-śakti*),
generate their respective substances when combined, like two gems joined together.
Just as a single reflection is pervaded by the states of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, so too,

through the predominance of the sixfold aspects therein, that which is characterized by the emergence of the predominance of knowledge is called the "inner instrument" (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of the mental intellect (*mānasabuddhi*).
And because of the collective nature of activity, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest, characterized by a fivefold body, arise in this way:
from each of the elements, two sense organs are produced individually, due to the distinction between the powers of knowledge and action. This is for the purpose of the instruments of knowledge.
May the fivefold sense organs of knowledge and the fivefold organs of action, which are intent upon performing their respective functions, as well as their presiding deities—
beginning with Indra and the others— who are preeminent in the powers of knowledge and action, flourish through the vigor and strength of those respective [deities].

The senses that delight in their respective objects, such as sound and the rest, as well as those that grasp the objects of action, such as speech and the rest, are all described as being non-different [from the Self]. This is because of the nature of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), and because they are pervaded by its form.
Like the strings of a lute appearing as a single form, the manifestation of various effects— such as the multitude of musical notes— is said to be the Supreme; that very same manifest object,
when perceived through the lens of individual distinctions, is the adjunct of the individual soul (jīvopādhi) within both the collective and the individual.

It has been determined that those elements, being as they are, are incapable of producing the stream of experience without a body as the locus of experience and objects as the objects of experience; therefore, being impelled by the karma of the living being, they become quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*) in order to manifest in gross form, respectively.

And those five gross elements, having been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta) and possessing a coarse state, known as "embodied" (mūrta), through their throbbing and mutual intermingling, produce individually a substratum that serves as the locus of experience; and that very thing is called the body of the senses.
In this regard, here the body of the gods has sattva as its predominant quality, that of humans has rajas as its primary quality,

and that of animals and plants has tamas as its predominant quality; likewise, both in this world and the next, there are forms that are pleasant and terrifying due to the experience of their respective opposites.

Above the Unmanifest (avyakta), through downward delusion, there are fourteen realms known as the worlds (bhuvanas), which— like the walls of a house— are composed primarily of the portions of sattva, rajas, and tamas, augmented by internal subdivisions;
these objects of experience are also "severed" [by the sword of knowledge] during the rending of insentience.

All this—the eternally risen [consciousness], the insentient objects such as jars and so forth—is proclaimed by that form of the Supreme Bliss as it has arisen; it is designated as the "Cosmic Egg" (*brahmāṇḍa*), as the "Virāj," and as the "embodied" (*mūrta*). In the former case, within the non-embodied entity, there is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

He is primarily called *Hiraṇyagarbha* by the wise, and is also described as the *Sūtrātman* (the Thread-Self) because he is the locus of the primary object of meditation, namely *kriyā-śakti* (the power of action). Such is the view of the Upaniṣads. Furthermore, the sequence of creation is the reverse of this, which is the sequence of dissolution according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The sections beginning with "Birth" (Janma-khaṇḍa) need not be accepted as separate, because everything is but the play of Consciousness; nothing has ever been born, and for that which is unborn, what is there to dissolve? Thus, from this One alone, the various sections such as the "Sword" (Khaṇḍa) and others arise, providing a vision of all paths, just as in the case of fish and other beings within bodies enveloped by water.

The power of leaping onto paths and perceiving what is visible; likewise, the eagerness to strike with wings that, though hairy like those on the left hand and other parts of the body, are shaped like swords; and the sudden dragging away of snakes from afar, even from a great distance.

Just as those with harsh throats and hoarse voices break [food] into pieces by their breath, or as even with a delicate tongue one looks for meat from afar with eyes raised far ahead; or just as the scent alone is inferred even from a distance regarding the body of a cow.

Wandering through various regions, such as when parrots, cakoras, pigeons, and the like digest substances like stone within their bodies and consume charcoal; or as when partridges, śārikās, and other birds,
having been nourished and placed near a measuring vessel, produce a whistling sound with their voices.
And there is conversation as among those born of one's own parents;

the mutual nourishing of one another elsewhere; and just as there are mosquitoes and the like upon the body, or as there is the production of abundant sounds within the body, so too are there [distinctions] among the various species of grasses and the like.
Just as the bees and other creatures of various species seen directly in bodies may resort to a connection with those bodies, so too does that one Self, though being one alone,
assume various forms in many bodies according to its own particular delusive sports in each respective way.

Whether with a portion or without a portion of my own power, he recognizes me; indeed, even for one who has resorted to a body vastly longer than mine, the influence of another is difficult to discern, as it is manifested through the specific distinctions of each individual's own sphere of experience.
But for me, who am bodiless, how could there even be a possibility of experiencing an influence?

For one whose mental faculty has utterly transcended all things, there is no longer any distinction between qualifier and qualified; and even when the exclusion of qualifiers and the qualified has been perfected, I alone remain as the One, devoid of a second, whether as the "other" or as the "self."
In some places and at other times, another person—even one who is not myself—appears through the play of great illusion (*mahāmāyā*).
Thus, I perform this dance neither in that manner nor in that [other] way; my excellence cannot be fully grasped even by those possessed of abundant wealth.
In all things such as forest grasses and cities, which are my own nature, I alone— whose true essence is consciousness and bliss— move about by my own sovereign power through that very reality;
this play of the worlds is but a single fraction of me, the one.

I produce a creeper even upon stones— a creeper that generates various manifesting resources and is enchanting with ever-new artistic charms; just as the Nandana garden manifests even upon the peaks of the divine mountain, so do I manifest [this] even within the water.
I kindle the sacrificial fire; and just as in the ocean,
I cause fire to blaze within the branches of trees and other objects even without contact with fire,
and I draw forth fire from sun-crystals and similar sources even though it is not present there.
I cause drops of water to burst forth even from moonstones and the like; indeed, as if from boiling [substances],
I cause sapphires and other gems to appear, and even from the earth, I bring forth young grass-blades and sprouts of *vāḍva* reeds.

By means of the movement of sound through the clouds that have smeared and spread across the sky, I shall cause the hosts of planets to move here and there with their fixed courses, as if they were reflected images upon the vast pathways of the heavens, like those upon the grounds of a city.

I produce from the waters of the ocean various-colored bubbles, possessing the power of the delusion of rising foam and shimmering with radiant light; and I draw forth from without the highly precious moonstone, endowed with exceedingly pure luster.
Just as pearls are released from oyster shells that contain worlds within them,
so too do I manifest straight branches from seeds whose forms are not crooked; and even from those very seeds which are most hard and devoid of vessels, I bring forth [the fruit].
The structure of the cosmic egg is surrounded by petals whose subtle channels are difficult to perceive through the senses;

it is enveloped by the creative power of eternal fire, more solid than even the hardest stones and yet more delicate than the finest filaments of a lotus flower, composed of various colors and minerals.

From the frost that consists mostly of water, I produce captivating heaps of jewels; likewise, being perfectly independent, I generate from the sun-stone and moon-stone gems of incomparable quality. Even from a soft lotus stalk, a thread is spun.
A certain being, whose body was composed of the finest iron ore and was exceedingly hard,
blazed forth with intense light even from the fuel of deformed wood; he was about to kindle the embers of Rohitāśva’s chariot.

I manifest various flowers— resplendent even from seeds devoid of fragrance, possessing an experienced abundance of supreme excellence, honored by their intense scent, and causing longing in the bees— and which, though colorless, are worthy of description in many colors.

To those whose experience of the ultimate has reached its limit— those who do not chew upon the colors of wealth, who are praised by the virtuous, and who swallow up the very measure of the supreme, sudden, and most exalted greatness— even from these most subtle [objects], there arise vast fruits.

Beholding within those [trees] fragments of his own body-forms, filled with various flavors that were more delicious to taste than even the most exquisite delicacies, and seeing from even the insentient cow-dung a multitude of small creatures such as goats and oxen in immeasurable numbers;

Relying upon him, I cause to live those devoid of the states of living and non-living; through the realization of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), I produce from the body of that Supreme Person—even though it has transcended all states—those who possess a constant state of dullness, such as nails, hair, and so forth, by means of the method of non-dual supreme bliss which is to be contemplated. What else could even the Supreme Brahman do?
Down to the level of an ant, I do not fail to perceive the various gradations of the letter *ka*— whether intense, moderate, or mild—
by means of the supreme grace of my all-powerful strength that swallows up every manifestation;
for they are indeed the locus of the great wonder of supreme aesthetic confusion (*vibhrama*).
I fashioned from various forms of edible food— whether it had been consumed or not—

the form of fleshless entrails; and those [entrails], having become a mass of flesh with bodies of distinct red, yellow, black, and white hues, were brought here by me through the opening of my mouth.

I lead away the strength of his fat and marrow; alas, I consume even the heap of bones produced from his own flesh; I restore him to life by means of the marrow-born [substance], and I present even the digestive fire with an oblation of all my own self as fuel.

I shall reveal that which is the refuge of ever-shining splendor and power, which, by being perfectly within all things, is devoid of the state of concealment and possesses its own innate form; which is inseparable, and whose supreme form is like a wonderful mass of downward-pointing flames— just like the form of the Supreme Brahman.

The Lord is always capable of performing, knowing, withdrawing, and protecting everything— whether it be with form or formless, the cause of infinite bliss, the accumulation of causes such as the syllable *ma*, immortality, equanimity, and non-appropriation.

Thus, the discourse on cause and effect is in vain, propounded by the ignorant through their own false intellects as an improper path; for even in one whose qualities have transcended all things and who is the supreme refuge of all powerful attributes, there is no reckoning of the threefold qualities (guṇas).

O you who shine with curiosity for the eternal, I alone am sufficient to summon that entire multitude of tasks belonging to my own sovereignty; I do so without requiring any collection of external causes, in a momentary flash of all-encompassing vision.
Thus, for one who abides in this very state— the Lord of Kalāṅga, possessing the power of Mahāmāyā,

wherein the mass of supreme bliss has risen and spread extensively, and which is free from the delusion of fragmentation— the individual soul (jīva) is established as capable of the activities of both the moving and the unmoving.
Although he has attained the state of being composed of the light and awareness of the supreme bliss that is eternal and innate, yet—
by virtue of being animated by the limitation imposed by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) superimposed upon himself—
he assumes multiplicity and partakes in a manifold creation, like one whose life-breath consists of division.

Certain great souls, whose nature is that of the Lord, possessing an abundance of qualities such as omniscience and the like, and endowed with infinite and vast powers, disregard the entire multitude of other living beings and take delight in their state of liberation.

Through each and every such activity, as if having attained oneness with Him, they are eternally content because the agitation caused by the failure to recognize the Supreme Lord within their own selves has been destroyed; thus,
even though they are limited like the four-faced Brahmā and others, they abide in the immeasurable locus that is the substratum of Māyā.

Residing both internally and externally, these highly deficient conceptualizations— well-known as the forms of the *oṃ* syllable and other such phonemes, and manifesting first as the nature of the *kalās*—
are like the states of dissolution within the *piṇḍas*, melting away due to being overwhelmed by the drinking of the supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*).

Just as the life-force (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), and the intellect (*buddhi*), though arising first, do not persist for long even if somehow preserved— being perishable merely through the experience of breath,
characterized by that very moment, like the physical mass of a newborn human infant.

Certain individuals, such as Āruṇi and Māṇḍavya, are capable of maintaining their original nature even when born [into a different womb]; like Paraśurāma and others, they remain for a long time within the entire body,
free from the sorrow of defeat, even when that body is destroyed, just as one remains unperturbed by the destruction of its bones and other parts.

Some who are worthy of being known through their secret abiding are neither known nor perceived, just as the deities presiding over the senses— such as those of the quarters and the wind— are not seen despite their presence,
because they are like the blazing digestive fire within the stomach that is not visible when the body is intact.
Within their respective bodies, there are always certain forms such as *k*,

*p*, *s*, *t*, *l*, *kṣ*, *r*, *b*, *h*, *y*, and so forth, which are like vowels and consonants; these, along with the organs of perception such as the eyes, end with the letter *m* and include the letters from *a* to *ḥ*.

Some, such as certain Kinnaras and Gandharvas, are clever in recitation, reading, and so forth, like speech and other such faculties; some have extremely terrifying forms, like the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas, and others; and some possess very gentle appearances, like anger and other such states in the world.

Just as some, such as the gods, are elevating like knowledge and contentment; just as some, such as Brahmins, are purifying through their very sight like the mouth and other parts of the body; just as some, such as dog-cookers (outcastes), have become untouchable like the anus and other parts of the body; and just as some are proclaimed as objects of meditation—so too [is this].

Just as the distinguished host of gods, beginning with Khuvāha, reside within one's own body through the intellect that perceives them as virtuous, so too others remain on the side of what is to be abandoned, such as serpents and the like, which— like unwholesome food— cause various diseases in the body;
and yet there are certain things that are most certainly to be accepted, such as great medicinal herbs and elixirs, just as they are in one's own body.

Just as wholesome food and the like, which are accepted by oneself as causes of health, [are not rejected], so too some— such as the former gods and others— even while hating their own source of origin, [do not reject it]; and likewise, others who have become one's own limbs do not reject that limb, even if it is like a disease produced from within themselves.

Just as cats and other creatures that harm their own offspring do not observe any restraint when crushing them with their rows of teeth or striking them with their tongues; and just as certain small insects, being born inferior, do not observe restraint; and just as certain [beings], like hair and nails, exist merely as a transformation of form once they have been measured out and cast off.
Just as those possessing a body, such as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and others, existed in the past, so too do others exist now;
and just as there are causes for certainty— such as one liberated while living, one who has realized Śiva,
or an omniscient one like Rāma— and so forth.
Having likewise dispelled conceptual constructions and volitions— just as [the Lord does] through the cause that is the condition for that [creation]— these [powers],
though devoid of my own specific portions, manifest as the emanation of manifold forms by taking on portions of the One. There is no one among them who...

Through the grace of Maheśvara, having become one whose bonds of *paśu* (the bound soul) have been rendered inexhaustible [i.e., severed], and having become a lord who has awakened from the great night-slumber of ignorance, she herself overcomes the supreme primordial ignorance; she is that *Savitṛ*, the most excellent, the cause of supreme bliss.

The one of supreme merit experiences that which consists of supreme light and awareness; and through that experience, even the false hope— shaped like a cat— that is called "saṃsāra" and falsely constructed by Śācikā,
becomes utterly vain.
Furthermore, being entirely powerless and dependent, he receives [the body] from somewhere, by someone, and for some reason; yet he is free from all fear,
the embodiment of pure consciousness alone, attained, indestructible, with all activity ceased,
possessing unbroken bliss, and utterly pure.

Because he shines as the sovereign empire of his own poetic words, having cast off the perception of those various bodies and so forth, and remaining as nothing but his own true nature, he rejoices as one who has made the state of the Supreme Lord his object— even while engaging in worldly activity through the delusion of identifying with everything from the sun down to the tips of the hooves [of cows].

For him who has become that [Self], the knot of the heart is rent asunder; all dualities, the intensity of egoism regarding the body and so forth, and the notion of duality within himself are severed.
The Ancient Supreme Person shines forth. Each and every thing, existing everywhere, is entirely everything.

All karmas, which are the false causes of agony at the vital points [of existence], are exhausted in order to experience the power of one's own sovereignty; and through that exhaustion, he alone is Śiva, he alone is Viṣṇu, he alone is the one capable of manifesting the supreme, intermediate, and lower states of Yoga.

Brahmā, the Great Illusion, the one who renders the world formless, whose own nature is the fourfold sound, the sovereign of his own station, he who has reached the very end of all conceptualizations beginning with the primordial cause, the destroyer of the fierce power of the constituent parts of time, the cause of the grace of spiritual perfection, the causeless one who fashions himself through that very state of Time— he is indeed the embodiment of knowledge and bliss.

The moon, with its fresh rising of moonlight and a sight that brings delight, is he alone; he who has transcended the vital breaths and is the very life-force of even the *prāṇa*; he alone is the destroyer of the great delusion that causes the wandering in the mass of darkness, the supreme boat for crossing over; and he alone is the internal fire that burns the fuel of ignorance.
He whose delight is in the dissolution of all manifested forms, whose nature is the light of knowledge, who possesses the splendor of the surface of the earth as his sacrificial offering,

and who shines in the supreme state, the highest heaven— he alone is the Great Indra; he alone is the means for attaining the joy, satisfaction, and exalted state of praise through the practice of wandering in search of liberation in the Supreme.

O Lord, he who has been consecrated by the objects of the senses, yet having directly realized this very Self through discernment, is victorious— though his own nature was obscured by ignorance— as that very discernment triumphs by means of its departure from the wondrous fetters that delude the bound soul (paśu).

For that supreme Lord, there remains no discourse concerning contagion and the like, nor any cause for ascending or descending; nor does any mental cultivation (bhāvanā) esteemed by those of limited intellect arise for him who has realized the non-existence of worldly becoming, nor even [the practice of] ākhuyāna and so forth.

His mind, having transcended the sense of "mine" through the enjoyment of worshiping various hosts of deities, becomes possessed of progressive and powerful strides; nor is there any discourse capable of describing his nature, for it is known only through his own innate experience.

"I am Brahman; I am the All, the Self, the Self-born, the Source, the Lord, devoid of all commands"—for one who has thus emerged [from the state of duality], no reasoning whatsoever remains, for he is free from the very notion of reasoning and its lack.
Nor is any investigation appropriate for him, as he has transcended the investigation of others and the movement within those [objects of thought].

The sphere of his mind is the movement of his own self-nature throughout the moving and the unmoving; he especially acts as the locus of desire, yet he does not rely on the pride of body and so forth, which are joined with a collection of limbs and parts belonging to this state that has been destroyed.

For one who has directly realized the mind that is free from designations, even the Arhat cannot satisfy the distinction of his experience— that a certain new meditation on the elements, such as the lower, middle, or higher stages, is the cause for attaining the union of the principles of yoga, transcending all objects of meditation.

The sixteen supports consist of the nature of fortitude; having withdrawn the assembly of elements, beginning with the five gross elements and space, along with their respective qualities, she who uplifts them becomes the certain retention of that particular concentration. This is eternally "Om," "Svaḥ," one's own Self alone—the Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.

For one who constantly and everywhere restrains [the mind] with the thought "I am becoming Brahman," there is the supportless foundation of all things; for such a one, the discourse of support and supported is utterly destroyed, as is its own excellent nature, and no effort of mantra-recitation is joined to it— neither grass, forest, nor mountain.

For one who, through his own contemplation, recites the mantra of his own nature even on all the planes (bhūmis), and who contemplates the eternally present "I-ness" in all arts, there will be no future connection with anything else through yoga,
as he is completely satisfied by the bliss arising from the recognition of his own Self.
The characteristic of the state of equanimity toward success and failure is to be defined as follows:

for one who is illuminated by yoga, who has transcended the security of worldly attainment (*yoga-kṣema*), who is unfit for the union of separation, and who possesses neither union nor separation— even in caves, forests, or the world, from the tips of his hooves down to the end of his tail.
For one who, through the absence of itching and shame, has contemplated the assembly hall and other such places as being like a forest,

and who contemplates all objects of the body and so forth as being essentially like ashes— being invigorated by vigor and constantly intent on the contemplation of smearing oneself with earth and ashes;

Nor, like earth, ashes, incense, or the infusion of medicinal herbs, does he possess by his very nature an endurance of cold, wind, and heat, since he is one who endures everything, who has transcended the pleasant and the unpleasant, and who has abandoned all conceptualization regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten.

And the equality regarding what is edible and what is inedible is said to be like that of a boar and others; it is not due to being under the influence of delusion, nor is it because of eating grass, water, and so forth, but rather because of dwelling in the dense forest of this world.

The forest and its groves are a dwelling and a source of consolation like that of deer; they are the constant playground for one whose delight is in solitude and whose rest consists of peace, captivating the mind through the abandonment of both food and fasting.

For one who is eternally satisfied by the consumption of all objects of experience gathered through the vastness of his own mind, for such an unattainable being who perceives equality everywhere, there can be no longing for the state of a frog, fish, or other such creatures resulting from their placement in the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers.

The determination of the wise, which removes the suffering of the virtuous and brings forth vigor, becomes a constant discourse on the nature of water-dwellers for one who is concealed within his own majesty;
yet for one whose mind is satisfied with the past and who has made the self alone his own, it never occurs.
The manifestation of his own bliss through the recitation of words and so forth by this one, who is the source of universal delight and free from delusion— like that of a parrot or a maina—
is a singing of sweetness arising from the gestures of his beautiful throat, according to the threefold method, which transcends the hearing of others.

Whether at the beginning, the end, or the middle, his investigation of the collection of musical notes (*svaragaṇa*) is such that nothing he performs fails to be captivating; nor is there anything that, being refined by the three *bhāvas* and manifested, does not constitute a complete dramatic representation (*abhinaya*).

Being struck, it does not for even a moment display its fourfold pleasant movement— consisting of the motion of its trunk, hooves, and other limbs— with modesty toward Ānanda; nor does it restrain the movement of the mind-horse of the respective deity of the musical instrument when struck, for that [mind] has already been defeated by itself.

The intense pricking of thirst for the meaning of those words is not at all able to make manifest this innate supreme bliss. Words are not independent; whatever is beneficial to the intellect or whatever latent impression (vāsanā) is considered fit, that meaning which is expressed through speech is [the true] meaning.

Even all the foremost of the gods and others, desiring to worship at his feet— which are uniquely distinguished as the source of infinite and unsurpassed bliss— have bathed in all holy places with that very same [water] which is the essence of all sacred sites;
by him alone has the great Lakshmi been overcome.
He alone is the foremost among the great sages; he alone is the composer of all literary works composed in both prose and verse.
Consequently, he is celebrated through various narratives, and by the mere recitation of his name, a devotee becomes purified. By him alone [was] Mount Meru...

He who made the earth, beginning with the mountains, and likewise the seven oceans; he who, having performed all sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, became capable of making all the gods and ancestors one with himself;
he alone, by his very glance, produces supreme joy for the wretched people.
He is the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) skillful in bestowing the fruits of all aspirations;

by his very food at the śrāddha and other rites, there is great honor for the ancestors, and he effects their rescue from the hells. This alone is his charming quality: that he is the leader who guides them each according to their own [destiny].

He alone is the cause of supreme satisfaction for those whose inner faculties are agitated by desire; He alone purifies all the lineages (kulas); He alone is the kinsman of the distressed and the weak; He alone is ever-risen, intent upon bestowing repeated contentment upon those who are overwhelmed by anxiety.

He alone is the instructor of innate wisdom endowed with supreme reasoning; he is the one who establishes the ultimate stability for those whose minds are distracted by agitation. All those blinded by delusion do not attain the light; yet, by becoming truly awakened, even while existing, they become the truly existent. Be!
He alone is the source of rebirth-lessness; he alone is the object of worship for the three worlds; by his grace alone, O Viśvambhara, even this entire earth becomes meritorious;
he alone is the knower of the supreme reality; and among all these—mother, father, and others—he alone is the most blessed.
In those scriptures, he is perpetually renowned as the foremost of ancient men; his majesty is accumulated through constant honor,

and being free from the delusion of succession and non-succession, his very repose in the delight of his own Self is the process of transmission for one who is devoid of the notions of "far" and "near" regarding all objective entities.

For him who has renounced all ritual action through such deliberation, in whom the expansive sense of selfhood— which consists of the very cultivation of the thought that "I am the body" regarding all wealth and possessions— no longer flickers even at every step, his state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*) alone is the performance of the highest of all true actions.
The very perception of one's own ego within this mass of fears such as death, disease, and desire is itself the state of non-ego;
the very contemplation through one's own experience is the forgetting of all existence and non-existence; and the very manifestation of the supreme reality that transcends words is [the goal].
The recollection of that [reality] and the dissolution of the mind, intellect, and so forth, is one's own innate, excellent intelligence;
it is the perfect discipline (*susamaya*) consisting in the non-perception of all temporal conventions, both with and without remainder,
and the disregard for activities associated with a master and the like.
Thus, his state of being a doer of good deeds is independent of rebirth in heaven and such; his true goal is the attainment of a virtuous state.

For him, who is filled with joy through the subsiding of both anger and attachment, non-attachment itself is the highest praise. And indifference toward the manifestations of ever-new mental states is his great gain, which transcends all else.

Furthermore, by means of the pair of seed-syllables (bījayuga) of Carcaka, he repeatedly returns to that very Mātṛkā— the forest of the supreme arising— through the intentness of continuous contemplation upon his own state,
becoming filled with the flavor of an uninterrupted flow.

His method of non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) consists of the emergence of supreme bliss, which is to be perceived by the vision that illuminates the entire path of the world composed of the grasped and the grasper— a path that transcends the states of loud recitation, whispered recitation, mental recitation, and muttered recitation, and which is ever-fresh and the nectar of supreme awakening. Wherever [this occurs]...

When one's own object is well-attended, the mind becomes thus without support, or with support; therein alone, the very stability of the intellect regarding the convention is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*),
which is characterized by a denser emergence and is devoid of the maintenance of a fixed position, as well as by movement and wandering.

I am my own self, experiencing all those various and non-distinct particulars through my innate experience— which is characterized by withdrawal, exertion, and the state of being devoid of objective existence, and which consists of the essence of aesthetic flavor— unimpeded by the constant flow of my own internal concentration, and somehow united with that very experience.
In the very act of cultivation, as each respective moment arises in its own time,

he does not conceptualize duality within himself; for one who is free from such conceptualization, there is the fulfillment of the state of the supreme, most delightful knower, which is non-dependent and whose ultimate reality is unconditioned.

O dear one, through the practice of *kumbhaka* (retention), *smṛti* (mindfulness), *tṛṣṇātīta* (transcending desire), and *gati* (movement), there is the threefold *prāṇāyāma* characterized by the non-perception (*asana*) of all duality and separateness;
this is indeed the self-restraint that brings about the cessation of desire, delusion, fatigue, and the like, within one's own inner nature.

Everywhere, his very essence is the immersion in the state of equal flavor (samarasatā); through the realization that transcends success and failure, he is born with the noble knowledge of the supreme designation; and by means of this accomplishment, all accomplishments are established for him through mere earnestness, as his own limbs are merely the movement of what is desired.

The salutation here is to one's own chosen deity, and there is no going anywhere else; this is the manner of circumambulation. One's own beloved is the external sacrifice, and the attainment of that state is the very essence of it.
His internal sacrifice is the constant flow of the multitude of stories concerning his own beloved;
his attachment to the recitation of various hymns of praise and the like is merely a lack of concern arising from his own will;
and his absorption, consisting of supreme rest, is the perception of all that is visible solely as the Supreme Vision.
The very act of making itself its own object is its true perception; it is ever-new through its own ever-new manifestations.

In whatever manner and wherever it may be, there is neither dependence on nor independence from existence or non-existence; its movement remains without distinction across all those various states, whether manifest or unmanifest.

For this one who knows the supreme distinction of the pairs, even states such as laughing, weeping, and dancing are themselves particular forms of *mūrchā* (ecstatic absorption). This is the infinite progression of infinite names, which satisfy the infinite beings throughout the infinite universe through infinite modes of expression.
The Play of the Thousand Names: By contemplating all those various collections of external and internal objects in one place, this [text] is indeed the supreme peace for him.

And for one whose immeasurable and steady joy has been liberated through the *tvaṃ-pada* or the *tat-pada*, wherein the secondary meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is subsumed elsewhere, there is the dissolution of the duality of the splendor of self-awareness; it is a single arising, eternally manifest, and self-existent.

And for those perfected ones who constantly offer the oblations of all sense-objects into the fire of consciousness, there is a perpetual sacrifice accomplished without effort; through the very tasting of the natural, unartificial *samarasa* (equal flavor) of each and every unprecedented object, [the fruit of] the sacrificial vessel and so forth is attained.

The procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*homaprakriyā*) is simply the offering of the existence and non-existence of various things into the state of one's own Self; it is the removal of the agitation caused by the rules and steps of self-offering and mental resolve, and this is the *upahāra* (offering) consisting of the Vedānta.

The innate intellect (*sahajāmati*), which is the irreproachable and supreme accomplishment, is indeed my state as the Great Lord (*maheśvara*); this very state of being a Great Māheśvara is intensely vibrating and shines forth everywhere from itself.
It shines most intensely. This state of never having depended on anything else is precisely the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).

The knower of the Self, whose very nature is the most stainless and expansive strength consisting of the supreme grace of the discernment of vital essence (*ojas*), crosses beyond sorrow; he knows Brahman and becomes Brahman itself. For him, there is no purpose whatsoever here through what is done, nor through what is left undone—not merely regarding worldly activity, but even regarding its engagement.

Acting solely for the sake of favoring the worlds, he dwells with the firm bonds of karma and other fetters born of worldly activity completely dissolved; indeed, through the attainment of the supreme state, he never again falls under the sway of the demoness of *māyā*, which occurs only upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* and the rest.
When the perfection of self-knowledge has been attained without conflict, at that very moment,
upon the falling away of the physical body, one is liberated while still embodied (videhamukta); this is the formless yet all-encompassing nature of the innate self as declared by the Supreme Lord.
Freed from all forms, he worships the supreme form, which is devoid of the collection of agents and the like, and is the foremost of all; yet, while a small remnant of *prārabdha* karma remains,
although he is omnipresent and touches upon all visible objects through the worldly dealings of the body and so forth, he remains the very nature of Brahman.

Thus he is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*), characterized by a specific mode of life consisting primarily of supreme bliss; having himself always been utterly liberated through the dissolution of all distinctions regarding every state, he is capable of liberating others as well, by means of his own stainless vision and so forth— this indeed is he.

Just like Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others, even while performing actions, he remains entirely untainted; for it is observed that there is a connection with dissolution through knowledge regarding those various previously ordained actions which occurred during the period of ignorance.
Once knowledge is attained, for one who always perceives everything as being of the very nature of Brahman, [no action] is prescribed.

Furthermore, because there is no fruit for an action that consists of the disjunction of fetters, it is like the sexual pleasure of a barren woman; and it is like a snake that has been thoroughly understood—
even if painted in a picture and possessing its characteristic playful movements— it is incapable of producing fear.
Likewise, even when the rope has fallen and is somehow impaired by the delusion that it is a double-tongued serpent,
there is no further production of fear; his vital breaths are not like [ordinary] breaths,
nor is his mind and so forth like the mind, nor are his senses like [ordinary] senses, nor is his body like a [physical] body.

Remaining thus, this one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) [shines] like the Lord of the universe; though immersed in his own body and so forth, he is as if not immersed by virtue of his mastery; though possessing a mind, he is as if mindless; though wandering through the delusion of all worldly activities, he is intent only upon his own divine play, and shines as the Supreme Lord over everything.
Indeed, this world is like a field of grain; whether it yields a harvest or not, the wise man—whether he be refined or unrefined—remains equal toward it and maintains compassion.
Whether there is praise or blame, neither the thought of union nor the thought of separation is capable of awakening his mind, for he has no concern for anyone, either in this world or the next.

There is no longing for sense objects. What need has he for a favorable occasion? Or, even if he knows the occasion, he is ignorant of the state of the knower, the known, and the knowledge; even though he is the supreme subject (*paramapramātā*), his mind is devoid of the conceit of validity regarding the means of knowledge and so forth. Or, even if he is a knower...
The supreme subject (*paramapramātā*), though not distinct from the states of the knower, the knowable, and the act of knowing,

and though devoid of the conceit of validity regarding means of knowledge and the like, conducts himself like a fool despite being endowed with the power of all sciences; even though he is eternally beyond destiny (*niyati*).
Having set aside that pride of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*),

though he is devoid of it, he performs all ritual actions through an attachment to their respective traditional practices; this very person, ever-arisen in joy, is indeed Brahman itself, even externally for the sake of people.
Through disciplined vision, he perceives existence within non-existence as consisting of the Residual (vaśiṣṭa);

though he has known the supreme object, his latent impressions regarding objects have completely passed away, and he beholds all things— such as sugar, rock-sugar, and pieces of jaggery— as being essentially of the nature of sugarcane juice.

He experiences only the pervasiveness [of the Self] everywhere; his sovereignty appears like a blade of grass, and gold and such appear like a clod of earth. Though he knows the born and the dead, he moves through them as one without distinction, falling and rising everywhere.

As if having just emerged from a difficult ordeal, he gazes upon everything with wonder: "What is it—whether past or yet to come in this world—that is capable of coloring his mind, which is free from all conceptualization and discrimination? And yet, he remains attached to everything."

Like a mental construction, it fondles itself; for one who sees everything with the eye of Brahman, there is no distinction between "other" and "one's own," nor does any mental fabrication circle around its own self like a whirlwind.
I am neither ancient nor new; I do not distinguish between you two.

To make known His immeasurable nature—whether as the ancient, the new, the measured, or the immeasurable—I shall describe that extraordinary, auspicious sequence of His, whose creation follows the proper order, and who is eternally free from effort or exertion in the three worlds, in heaven, or in the nether regions.

Though he is effortless, the worlds behold him as one who laughs; he laughs at everything without any cause for laughter, and everything appears to him like a fallen leaf. Constantly satiated by the delusion of experiencing his own awakened consciousness, he is free from the dense distinctions of enemy and friend, yet remains something indescribable.
Whether in a playground or a palace, in a thicket or at the onset of a deadly poison, in a kingdom or amidst the firm-minded, he regards friend and foe with equal indifference;
and with a mind as barren as a wasteland, he renders everything void, even the Lord of Speech himself, like one who is mute and speechless.

Even though he has transcended all diversity through his own hearing of the Supreme, he either conceives of all entities as diverse or does not so conceive; as if reeling from the savor of his own bliss,
he does not open his eyes at all, yet he perceives all this very slowly and gently.

With eyes closed, he is not even capable of doing anything; yet, though all that was done and is being done has passed him by, he accomplishes everything. Though beyond the range of all hearing, he brings everything within the path of the ears; and though devoid of the slightest movement of coming and going, they go here and there [to reach him].
Though devoid of personal intent, Śatānanda spoke something like Vāgīśvara (Bṛhaspati); though having cast off childhood, Saṅkara was like Caturmukha (Brahmā), possessing all auspiciousness;
and though the cause of the destruction of all, Mṛtyuñjaya was like Viṣṇu.
Though he is celebrated as Hṛṣīkeśa and possesses ever-shining supreme splendor,

that delighter of people, like Indra, is possessed of dense luster and established in the imperishable state; yet, though he is the one of great renown (Vṛddhaśravas) who manifests his innate nature as Indra everywhere, he is nonetheless a non-believer (Nāstika).

He does not pursue the fruits of karma; though he is the Moon, he is like Vināyaka, the remover of obstacles to duality and non-duality. Like Kumāra, he is a youth here, yet he is not situated in this world nor in the next; though he is fire, he is not [fire].

He whose calves are dark and whose gait is dark is indeed the Ever-Moving One (Wind), yet he is not the one who identifies with the vital breaths; he is the Lord of the Puṇyajanas (Yama), yet he is not the King of Kings; he is Death himself, yet he is not the one who inflicts punishment;
though he exists in a state of impartiality, he is not the King of the Departed; and though he is the Lord of Men and Rakṣasas, he is not the Lord of the Dead.
Though he is a great night-stalker (Mahāniśācara) and a sovereign of all aesthetic flavors (Sakalarasarāja), he is devoid of the noose (Pāśa);

though he possesses immeasurable wealth of merit (Puṇyadhana), his merit has vanished; though he is the supreme art (Parakalā) and a hero (Śūra), he is naked; though he is the sacrifice of all (Sarvamakha), he has lost his friendship with people; and though he is Samantabhadra, he is not as such [in this state].

The agent has departed, yet the action is not; the fruit of the action is not consolidated [into a self]. He is indeed the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) and the Guru; he does not speak anything that is not worth speaking, and he speaks with both gentle and non-gentle dispositions. Though untouched by these states, he is ever gentle. "I am Brahman"—this is the realization, this is the command.

He sports beyond the past; though free from attachment, he possesses graceful charm; though having transcended his natural state, he is innate; though his latent impressions are exhausted, his intention is pure; though devoid of the conceit of a body, he has taken on the form of the supreme formless Absolute; and though his ego has been suppressed, he shines with divine play.

Though he is the manifestation of the supreme ego, he is devoid of the vibration of differentiated existence; though he is the highest wisdom, he is not merely wise; though he is the whole, he is partless; though he is the Virāṭ, he is free from the conceit of being Virāṭ; and though his splendor is unsurpassed, he is neither Taijasa nor one afflicted by the state of dreaming.

Even one who has transcended the count of others, who rests in the fourth state (*turyapada*), and whose trembling has been cast far away, having realized his own vibration— no one can know in any way what he is like; he is not dead, yet there is no longer any fear of rebirth for him.
He who does not manifest as prior, transverse, or upward, nor as downward, nor in the middle; he who is neither delusion nor pride;

he who is both existent and non-existent, yet is the Supreme; he who is the Middle, yet being the Supreme is neither Middle nor Low; he who is indeed the Right, yet being the Right is that very same [Supreme] beyond that.

He alone is with beginning and without beginning; he alone is both prior and yet not prior; he is the direction of welfare and the Lord of all directions and objects, being without end even while having a western course;
he alone is below and not below, and he alone is above and in all that is above.

His supreme greatness is beyond description; he is the ultimate author of all narratives and the instructor even of those who know every branch of ethics. Thus, he does not fear death, nor does he fear living beings, nor spirits such as *piśācas* and *ḍākinīs*; he suffers no humiliation whatsoever from them.

When his heart is spontaneously and intensely attached to the Supreme Refuge, which is capable of removing those various miserable states of existence, what other instruction can there be for him who is the authority over all instructions?
Who else could describe the majesty of his own sovereign power?

He alone, whose own experienced majesties are known throughout the entire world, has cast off all delusion through his own speech; he alone is the creator of all illusions and he alone is without a second.

Even one who has attained his body through the mere renown of his own [status]— who else could possibly know that doctrine which has removed all other views? And everyone else, including Death himself, feels fear toward even a fraction of it.
Thus, that very [Reality] is the cause through its play of bliss—causeless yet the cause of all;

it is its own state, more delightful than anything else from every perspective; it alone is capable of bestowing those various excellent boons; though transcending the principles (tattvas) such as earth and the rest, it alone is the source of the emergence of each and every principle.

He is the one who effects the dissolution and disjunction of the fetters of worldly existence; moreover, no other is capable of knowing his experience, for even the supreme Lord is like a snake at the foot of such a one. Thus, this one is known as liberated while living, having realized the power of his own innate, nectar-like, and stainless strength.

At the moment of its first experience, this delusion—which sustains [the world]—is like a long-lost dear friend who, though always present, seems suddenly attained; yet it is as if he has been cast away by himself, his every thought having passed away. Oh, how the true nature of form is thus manifested!
She attains a state thick with the vibration of supreme bliss; having directly realized the nature of the pure,
formless, and singular Essence— which transcends all objects— she, as if praising her own Great Lord-Self, abides even in her second state.
Just as if summoned by that very sign, characterized by the radiance of consciousness, as it were by a glance from the direction of vision.
Salutations to You who are mine alone; salutations to me who am Yours alone.
Salutations again and again to You and to me, who are eternally one, though appearing as many.
Homage to the one who, through the striking away of qualities, appears devoid of qualities to the possessor of qualities;
homage to the Supreme Power whose qualities transcend the categories of both the possessor and the possessed of qualities.
Salutations to the one whose nature is both non-reality and reality, who transcends all principles (tattva),
and who is the very embodiment of reality itself, directly manifesting that reality in every state.
I bow to you, the sky-like expanse; there is no one higher than you for me, nor is there anyone beyond the supreme, because you are that supreme one—to that supreme you, I bow.
Through the vision of Śakti you are the Supreme Śakti; through the vision of Śiva you are that One alone;
and through the vision of the individual soul (jīva), both of these are you, whose nature is self-illumined.
Taking refuge in you alone, O Lord, each and every one goes wherever they must.

In this regard, you alone are the delusion of this [world], for you are indeed its delusion; O Lord, you are the light, and I am the light by means of yourself. There is not even the slightest difference between us two, whether we are considered as directions or as non-directions.
Throughout the long duration of my birth, where have you been, even though you are omnipresent?
From whom did this speech arise—through reasoning or through the absence of reasoning?
You have been touched, you have been touched! What visions do you see?
Seeing, the act of seeing, and the object seen—these are merely names; I am the Great Guru, the Supreme Self.
Whatever I know, in that I abide; and whatever I do not know, in that too I abide.
You alone are the Knower—not knowledge, nor the object of knowledge, nor the conceptualization of a knower.
O Lord, how is it that even Your own Self— which is dearer than the beloved, dearer than life, and dearer than the very soul— has been forgotten by You, deluded as You are? Indeed,
it is only when illumined by Your radiance that intellect and the other faculties shine forth.
How can there be existence therein, and how can there be a self-nature spoken of in that very same place?
O Supreme Lord, this is indeed a great wonder:
that Your own Self, though endowed with its own play, remains hidden from Yourself.
In this world as well as in the next, you wander like a leaf;
for one who does not laugh at the self and the non-self, there is no name.
This woman, who measures and is full of pride, has reached the state of being measured by the path of coming and going.
By my own will, I am that cognizer, Śiva, the remaining one, possessed of distinguished luster.
O Lord, you are eternally celebrated as Śambhu; why then is there no manifestation for me at this first occasion? O Protector, grant me through your power the manifestation of worldly existence.
Everywhere, at all times, for everyone, from every side, and in every way, he alone exists;
you are indeed he, O you who are not non-existent, nor non-non-existent, nor both, nor neither.
You are the supreme; you are not surpassed by another, nor are you surpassed by anyone else. You have existed as neither other nor non-other to yourself, by means of your own self.
This [world] is pervaded by the pervader through pervasion, and otherwise it is pervaded by that which is other than pervasion;
even the pervader, by its very movement, is for us nothing but the pervaded.
O Lord, why is even that which is fit for conversation not spoken?
By Your own will, O You of incomparable desire, You engage in conversations that are, in truth, no conversations at all.

In its stainless nature, it is neither by its own form nor by another; though possessing the splendor of the clearly defined peak of the mountain of the object to be characterized, it is yet beyond all defining characteristics.
Without this form of yours, what is the supreme power (parā-śakti) like? And with it, what is she like? Or how is she when neither exists nor exists?
How can Śaṅkara be carried by one who is devoid of the form of delusion?
Or how, O Lord of the gods, can he be carried by him along with that [delusion]?

The existence of objects occurs solely through His existence; likewise, the non-existence of those same objects occurs through Him. O Lord, You alone remain eternally one with Yourself as their manifestor.
If there is a mother, she knows her son; if there is no mother, she does not know him.
O, though you are devoid of the light of such mental cognition, you shine forth! Ah!
You are not the knower of yourself, nor are you the knower of another;
you are eternally the Supreme alone, the immutable knower who knows the immeasurable.
Though subtler than the subtlest, You are greater than the greatest; supreme even beyond the supreme, You are neither higher nor lower, yet the highest of all.
Even though it is always present before one's eyes, it is not perceived without its own grace,
just as the writing of Śiva is not seen without the application of collyrium.
O Lord, why do you weary yourself with such degrading conceptions regarding me? O Ishvara, why even trouble yourself; this very talk is itself a source of distress.
I see you as consisting of Māyā alone, and I am a vision of Śiva;
whether you are such as this or otherwise, there is no loss for me, who have cast off all growth.
On one side is demerit, and on the other is merit alone;
for you who know the two ways, tell us whether this act of yours is meritorious or not.
How can there be any movement— whether in pleasure, pain, or delusion— of the Great Lord, who is the supreme purifier among all purifiers, even when faced with improper action?
Where even the later Mīmāṃsā is surpassed by his Mīmāṃsā,
how could the earlier one prevail against such power?
How does one desire to understand one's own cause, which is *dhiṣaṇā* (the intellect)?
O Lord, even if one does not personally desire a discourse on the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*),
it arises from the dawning of the stillness of the vibration of extraordinary, great bliss.
Salutation to the Knower, the omnipresent one, who is both self-originated and beginningless.

O friend, here, there, and everywhere— even in the scriptures— salutations to that one who is both the perceived and the unperceived, who partakes in every moment, and who is the single, unique reality.
Salutations to Him who, like a sword, cuts asunder the dense forest of delusions consisting of the individual soul, ego, mind, and so forth; to Him who appears as the enemy of all [obstacles].
O Lord, how is it that conceptual construction is not destroyed by the creation of existence?
Even though it exists somewhere as something with form, how is it that it increases in any way whatsoever?
O Śaṅkara, how great indeed is this increase of yours,
which increases perfectly so that even the increase of decay serves only for further growth!
Those very memories that flow forth here as the expansion of memory— he, indeed,
perceives them by bringing the three times to their end.
Salutations to that skillful one who, in speech, mind, and thought, grasps all this without confusion regarding its activity.
Somewhere, someone, being the master within his own self,
creates himself by perceiving the forms of the construction of time within his own self.
Through whatever kind of body and whatever kind of vision, I perceive the limit of the distinction between the seer and the seen;
yet I do not see another Lord, resplendent with that glory of his own.
Whatever various perceptions appear as objects of your own vision,
O All-pervading Lord, they are manifested by you alone through the play of strength and weakness;
these are employed right here like the roles of an actor.
In your jesting, courtesy is eclipsed by the supreme splendor [of your nature].
O Lord, in whichever places here you conceal Your own form from the waters, in those very places,
O Master,
Your supreme and most wonderful courtesy shines forth as if it were a concealment.
O All-pervading Lord, that very Self, when manifested in the mind, appears as a duality for the sake of its own distinctness.
Why do I not bow to you who remain hidden in such and such ways?
And why do I not bow to that supreme manifestation of yours which is revealed in such and such ways?
Having recognized You, the Supreme Lord— the Knower who is known as the unsurpassed non-dual reality and the object of knowledge—
someone shall attain supreme bliss through this means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Out of supreme grace, I bow to you, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, who embodies the essence of all things and serves as the illustrative example for all philosophical views.
I bow to you, the one of great wealth, whose face never falters even in the three states of emotion, who is never led astray by any deceptive logic, and who is ever victorious over fear and kings.
How can one who has performed prostrations toward their own self be satisfied by the very act of making distinctions, as if toward a corpse?
Relying on my own power and strength, I bow to myself— the non-dual Maheśvara of vast body— by means of my own innate capabilities.
