Whether it manifests in various ways even in knowledge that is capable of action,
I bow to that which is devoid of external injunction and is the very mark of Indra.

We praise the Great Lord of Vital Breath (Mahāprāṇeśvara), who by means of his own consciousnesses—such as the vital breaths and so forth—animates the inert universe; who, through his own power, has dispelled the great delusion;
and who repeatedly fashions this world through his own volitions and conceptualizations.
I bow to the Lord of the Mind, whose accumulation of provisions is without origin and immeasurable.
I bow to Śiva, who is known by the wise as the momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna*) according to the Buddhists— He who brings joy at every moment through the five [senses]—
and who, because He is eternally full due to His perfection, is therefore the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
I bow to that Great Emptiness which, having been realized, remains as you.
Since there is nothing further to be known for him, how could he be a knower of another?
Take refuge in this Lord who is devoid of the state of being both the object and the subject of knowledge, and who is beyond the ignorant.
I bow to Śiva, the Great Lord of Action, by whom action has been destroyed, and in whom there is indeed liberation from action, apart from the manifestation of the agent of action.
Even for him who possesses time, this [Lord] appears effortlessly as his own very time;
free from the calculation of time and so forth, he is the victorious Lord of Time.
He does not cease from the fivefold activity that constitutes his own nature;
though not a doer, he acts as if he were—a single Lord who is ever victorious.
I bow to that non-dual Great Enjoyer who, having himself assumed the manifold power of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, performs his divine play;
he for whom primordial nature (prakṛti) remains unchanging even as it unfolds among the principles (tattvas).
He indeed [attains] that Great Person within the supreme reality of the primordial nature.
Having abandoned the conceptualization of afflictions and the like, he illuminates all those mental states through his own majesty; may that omniscient Śiva indeed [grant] [blessings].
I bow to that Vāsudeva, the supreme teacher of teachers, in whom this world dwells and by whom it plays in such and such ways.
He who protects this very herd of cattle is its lord;
even those who offer oblations into the fire, following that mode of life, shall satisfy that powerful one.
I eternally sing that innate resonance, which is the basis upon which the various praised sounds separately converge toward a single meaning.
Even though he is eternally devoid of the conceptual constructions of Māyā,
those who have attained that supreme state do not return from the forest of Māyā, as if they were still under its influence.
I bow to Him who, having repeatedly illuminated the conceptualizations of "vision" and "creation," sports with His own people while being fully cognizant of the state beyond all conceptualization.
I bow to Him, the Lord who is non-dual and whose light is His own nature, who, though eternally and exceedingly near, appears as if far removed.
Victory to you, O Great Lord, the Self! You who transcend the designations of fullness and emptiness, O Lord of Fullness; though eternally empty, you are beyond even emptiness—be victorious!
This existence shines forth through devotion to Bhava, leading to auspiciousness;
for those beings who are perverted and lacking in fortune, it is a miserable birth.
This equality would dissolve into the "I-ness" through the cessation of delusion;
for the realization of that [equality], grace alone is the cause here.
What else do I not see now, or what else do I not hear?
I am the seer and the hearer, yet merged in otherness, devoid of the manifestation of objects.
I have taken refuge in that innate and peaceful one who possesses two powers,
by whom this world was effortlessly seen as having become like a mere mirage.
Victory to you, whose greatness pervades the greatness of the great;
victory to you, the imperishable one who makes the minute vast and the vast minute, and who is the mine of all virtues.
We are not [convinced] by this single word; you do not appear as one in that single word.
What word is there for its creation? Its greatness is beyond measure.
O Lord, for You who are beyond the number of the "incalculable," even the incalculable is not a number;
though all numbers are counted within You, may You, who are devoid of number, be victorious! Homage to the one who is higher than the highest, the Supreme, who extends beyond the supreme!
It also arises from another for others, and for another [self] as well.
Homage to you, the unique supreme reality, who is the grain for the entire teaching, the ruler of the entire teaching,
and the one who excels even the teaching through the excellence of reality.

Victorious is the Lord, who has become his own radiance, whose fame is cherished by all beings, who makes both the manifest and the unmanifest known, and whose renown extends through every path of all things.

What is there that is not you, since you are the all-pervading Lord who pervades everything? What is this world that appears as fragmented, when you are the entirety of it, possessing boundless majesty?
Indeed, you cannot even be described by speech, nor can you be bowed to even by the mind;
for you are fit to be described and honored only after one has abandoned even the distinction between "I" and "you."
Salutations to the auspicious one, whose nature is auspiciousness and peace, by whom,
when cast into it, the world-creator’s auspiciousness becomes as if infused with essence.
One's own self always triumphs as it attains various beneficial states;
yet even the Supreme Self appears as if it were another, wandering like a swinging pendulum between delusion and its cessation.
Playing with his own divine sport, his radiance shimmering and undulating,
the Lord Śaṅkara, having taken refuge in a certain supreme moon-like splendor, is victorious as the Self.
Victorious is this Supreme Lord, who, though possessing immense power, meditates upon the mass of non-dual bliss by means of taking recourse to duality.
O Lord of Mountains, you are the master of which scripture yourself? Having set aside everything that is subject to mastery, even Lakṣmī herself is not yours to command.
To you, both the audible and the visible appear; here, even that which is visible is indeed audible.
Therefore, for one possessed of dense wisdom, there is neither the audible nor the visible.
The velocity of the mind is indeed its wandering; for that [velocity] is its delusion.
How, then, could there be movement in the Lord, who is free from delusion and possesses a great intellect?
The intellect determines nothing without the wandering of the mind;
yet that wandering does not exist in You, O Lord. Therefore, the quality of determination belongs to neither of these two.
In whatever manner and wherever the mind and wisdom shine forth, that is indeed Your manifestation as the Lord, in that very manner and in that very place.
What is not done by that [self] where you are, and what is done by that where you dwell?
Is that which is uncreated truly created, or is it merely created by itself?
For this [Self], which is a single mass of light and whose own nature is bliss, what could possibly be an instrument? Or rather, is there no instrument at all?
If Bhāsiprabha is always conjoined with his own autonomy,
or if he is dependent on another, then what has been done, or rather, what has not been done?
Meditating moment by moment upon your equanimity toward all things,
I bow here to you, who are omnipresent— within me, within you, and throughout this pervasive power.
How can any distinction manifest here in your essential form, which is pure bliss?
By that same reasoning, what basis for it could possibly be distinct?
If that [subject] also possesses subjectivity by its own nature, then it would be mental;
therefore, since you alone are the one [subject] of this [object], by whom and for whom has it been conceptualized?
O Ānanda, being intensely pressed and reeling from the supreme nectar,
where, how, and from whence does he perceive that duality which is the state of seeing?
In this world, having become intoxicated, one forgets other thoughts; how much more so, then, would this moon, intoxicated by drinking its own moonlight, remember anything else?
Aha! This greatness of yours, your own consciousness, is ever-shining;
yet you do not know it, or rather, you display the humility of your own self.
If this is some kind of snare of illusion, do you protect it as nectar?
Or is it for the sake of knowing or not knowing its own true nature?
But I know that this illusion is not divided by anyone under a different name;
even by him it is not divided, for she is his own self—you are that very self.
How is it that you, though not lowly, accept play as if you were lowly?
Or rather, this face of yours is truly blessed, for it is the very mouth of Brahma’s sport.
Is there no name for You? Or is it that even a name does not exist? O Lord, O Ruler of Gods, are all names indeed "na" (negations)?
Do You shine as one who is truly nameless, or do You shine while possessing a name?
Whether there be joy or not, you are simply devoid of wisdom, regardless of how it may be.
Once you have somehow attained recognition, the state of being tossed on a swing may last for only a moment; yet, what remains is your own bliss.
O Lord of Gods, our worldly pleasures have perished here at the mere sight of you;
we are satisfied, having recognized your eternal blissful radiance.
O Great Lord, since you speak with your own charming and playful words,
why do I not caress you with my speech, as if with soft whistlings?
O Īśāna, dense mass of consciousness and bliss, victory to you whose supreme expansion is eternal!
O Self, manifesting as your own manifestation, victory to you, the expansion that is the expansion of all!
O God, Lord of Gods, having recognized you in every way from all sides,
I bow down, I bow down to you— this very vision of Śiva.
The single supreme form of this Brahman, having indeed attained the state of the *kiṅkiṇī* (the small bell),
appears as the one beautiful, primordial consciousness.
O Lord, this form of yours, which bestows all things, consisting of consciousness, bliss, and beauty, is formless; to whom would it not be worthy of salutation?
I bow with my own self within the self to that one Lord of the gods, who has attained the supreme state and shines forth through both external objects and ultimate reality.
The taste of the gateway to awakening has been obtained by me in you alone;
I shall count you as one only, for where else have I not wandered?
He who grasps the divine Speech, whose sole cause is the Śabdabrahman—
though it appears divided, its meanings are not distinct— that very Self-born Brahmā,
having attained the state of four faces, beholds the Veda.

May that very Blessed One, who at first created the diversity of pleasure, delusion, and suffering, now manifest through his various incarnations— displaying those wondrous and majestic deeds— with his supreme glory of eternal bliss.
O Nanda, he for whose sake this abode of the thirty gods exists with its hosts of celestial beings— that Indra, the lord of truth— is not even a footstep on the path.

O King, how is it that the wise man, though satisfied, does not immediately obtain you— the pervasive Purifier who is beautiful with light— as the cause [of his goal] through the performance of sacrifices?
O Lord, you who have reached the supreme state of restraint and withdraw these worlds,
you are indeed the impartial one who wields the sword against all creations composed of duality.
Having repeatedly struck down those various gods who were but fragments of passion, you alone remain;
O Great Night-stalker, you shine, for you are the unshakeable Lord of all.
O you who indeed dwell within the inert world by taking refuge in it—
this King of Tastes (mercury) is the conqueror and the master of that very world through his state of equilibrium.
Victory to the Lord of Great Vitality, the all-pervading and unshakable soul, whose single power alone shines as the support of the three worlds.
You, who are the seed-basis and the element, dear to the three eyes like a treasure;
you are this King of Kings, victorious, with a mind resplendent with light.

Having drawn forth the entire world, this Great God, resplendent with every auspiciousness, sports; he is the conqueror of the gods. Transcending the lofty void, the great path, he is free from fatigue.
You, who are the destroyer of darkness, are the Sun, whose portion is austerity.
By that through which this world is purified and shines even here in the night of distress—
O Soma, you who have quelled all darkness, do you not bear the nature of one born of noble lineage?
Though a member of a multitude, you are beyond counting; though a god, you are the refuge of the gods' powers.
You are a Yakṣa because of your power in sacrifice, and you are Śaṅkara because you extend (tanana) the state of being (sat-tva).

You are the lord of the Vidyādharas, yet because of your repeated negligence regarding your magic power, you have failed to protect the world; therefore, O All-pervading Lord, you must be my protector.
What is this that shines as the supreme person? What is this renown of "person"? It is merely the scent of various illusory forms, like the fragrance of a Gandharva city carried by the wind.
Since you bear a terrifying splendor through various limbs that manifest a dual nature, you are therefore this lordly Piśāca.
"O Guhyaka, you are indeed the Supreme Self, the all-pervading one who is known through right reasoning; therefore, this Parameśvara here is truly [the Supreme Self]."

Although there is the supreme accomplishment consisting of the realization of one's own self, as well as the various other accomplishments such as *aṇimā* and so forth, even a divine Siddha who has resorted to both of these— namely, the supreme Brahmic state and his own innate *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness)— still delights in the measurable world (*meyataḥ*).
Smeared with the conceit of being an element, he is like one who has spat upon an element.
Is it because you alone are the sovereign of these three worlds that this [world] proceeds? And why was that planet not struck down by him, since even a planet is not without its own confusion?
Since you take away the desire for rebirth and the like through the gift of the medicine that restores the dead to life,
you shine with a sweet luster as the physician of the heavens.
Having abandoned both knowledge and ignorance, you have resorted to supreme silence;
thus, O sage, you have become perfected, and even your human nature has been transcended by you.
You are the earth because you dwell within all; you are water because you manifest as distinct forms;
you are fire because you shine everywhere; and you are wind because you move everywhere.
You perceive the sky on all sides and that which is the movement of the planets; you are the region measured by space, and through your mastery, you are even the directions themselves.
You alone are the support of Śiva, and you are the supreme Lord who is the supported.
Even the act of placing [the fire] is your power; thus you alone appear as the Lord.
O Śivā, you shine as the state beyond, and you are this very light here;
in each and every place, you are that luminosity, both singlefold and manifold, eternally.

You possess nothing, yet you are everything; O Śaṅkara, you alone shine resplendently in all those various roles. You are present here and there, and you are the very light that illuminates each of those places.
From where and where do you not shine? You shine everywhere and from all sides.
Possessing a single, beautiful body with the touch of unsurpassed flavor,
Śiva shines upward, across, and downward by his own vision, in the middle, above, and below.
We bow down to that certain one who is beyond all recollection,
by whom even the Lord of the Immortals has been entirely forgotten.
Homage to Śivā, who is difficult to pierce and who pierces that which is difficult to pierce! Even this differentiation is she herself, who manifests spontaneously;
she who has transcended all forms and whose supreme state shines forth.
And I bow to this formless one, O Lord, who is the embodied form of those mortals.
Obeisance to the Lord who, having rendered the nature of self and other identical by cultivating the realization that the Self of all is one,
always shines as if he were both himself and the non-self, appearing like the sun.
O you who are beyond time, whose net is the manifestation of your own playful power!
O non-inert one, salutations to you who uplift the fallen and have become inert for the sake of others!
You alone are the self of both the non-inert and the inert; you are the one self of all.
O Knower of the Vedas, you have attained the supreme state; through you, and not apart from you, resides success.
You alone are that which is success, for one who knows this does not find failure.
Where, by whom, or what could be accomplished, since everything is achieved through your own inherent perfection?
The non-establishment of the other is itself the establishment of the other; in that which is eternally arisen and all-pervading, there is accomplishment free from both the goal and the means.
Let us worship this accomplishment, praised by the true perfected ones, through the grace of the Divine.
We worship that own light, which is both selfhood and otherness, yet is the very ground of Nandana;
it is entirely without distinction, yet is the ultimate remainder of all distinctions;
it is the great splendor in which every affliction has been cast away.
What is known when you are known? And what is known even when the Self is known? Knowledge is merely your delight; yet knowledge itself is you.
O Lord, by the gods who delight in evil, the sacrifice—which is a source of manifold distinctions that ought to be abandoned—has been performed;
yet, through Your grace, the being at the end of his limbs has bowed down. Today, false view is destroyed, and the vision of the Self has become fully awakened.
Wretchedness, which causes weakness, has vanished somewhere;
the artificial cause of discord, which pierces one's convictions, has set.
Elated by the power of His grace, I sing and I rejoice.
Today, this certain devotion, which is like the moonlight of one's own moon, shines forth;
by drinking from its nectar-essence, I have become free from the fever of worldly existence.
Thus, this [reality], which is supremely blissful and exceedingly beautiful as the ultimate truth,
remains endowed with a trace of non-dual power and is distinguished by devotion to you.
Today, through this discourse, action has been destroyed, as well as the improper action that follows from action;
you shine forth as the one who knows the nature of pure light, appearing as the self-measured Mother.
I am myself immediately liberated from the bondage that was conceived by me;
the very bond by which I was bound has been destroyed along with its mental fluctuations.
My own excellence is distinguished; today I am merely refined. I am liberated from liberation, just as liberation itself is liberated.
Just as the Gaṅgā, though flowing through three paths, has attained renown as being one alone.
I am the single-bodied Śiva, whose delusion is characterized by the atomicity of Śakti.
Today, this devotion of mine toward you surpasses even liberation;
for liberation and enjoyment both overstep their own established boundaries in the face of devotion.
I cherish my own self again and again as the supreme object of worship;
O Lakṣmī, you shall manifest of your own accord within me in an expansive form.
But having attained supreme skill, you somehow come to know me;
what is the use of my manifest form, and what is the use of my unmanifest state? Now, for me, all calculation regarding karma and the like has utterly perished.
Now, indeed, there is for me, who performs all actions, a state of freedom from action.
This very state of being actionless in every respect is indeed the performance of the first duty;
for what action do I not perform, and what is there that I do not do everywhere? By whatever innate desire I myself sport, [that is my action].
The very desire of the sattvic person is not merely desire; it has attained supreme dissolution.

The Śakti, consisting of all reality, shines with powerful radiance; she is both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā), consisting of the ultimate unity of a single reality. Just as various realities appear here in their true nature, so does she manifest.

O Lord, endowed with great majesty, your straightness appears to me as a lack of crookedness in your gait, free from the calculation of arts; likewise, your state of non-reliance is cherished by the character of the Possessor of Power.
Since that single seed which has grown here has come to be manifold through its own inherent nature, you alone, O Earth, are exalted by this abundance.
I bow to You, Maheśvara, the life-force who is the supreme cause of aesthetic delight for both the insentient and the sentient, and who brings about eternal awakening.
I bow to Pāvaka, the Lord of perfect radiance, who brings even the entire world consisting of all beings under his control.
He who spreads his own unerring nature both internally and externally,
having forever destroyed all destruction through his constant movement, is the conqueror of the wind.
You always shine everywhere in an expanded form;
you who, by your own nature and essential form, are the stainless essence and the sky.
Or rather, this certain living being, like a bee, wanders, sings, and dances within the slender lotus-stalk of the mind;
though seemingly liberated, it is not truly free.
I bow to you, O essence of the world, who have transcended the highest of the high;
you are free from all latent tendencies, yet the source of all tendencies, with all bonds destroyed.
In every case, that upon which attachment is experienced—
even by those who have attained extreme fickleness— is as if it were most steadfast.
The fulfillment of mutually bound states occurs through their mutual assistance;
thus, O Sattva, may you here attain victory, you who possess the essence of qualities exceeding the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Even one's own self and others are not perceived at all without You; I praise You, the celebrated Lord, who is form itself, yet not possessed of form.
I bow to that Lord of Touch, who is the touch of those who know touch, by means of whose cultivation of softness and other qualities within the objects of the senses, one attains his very being;
he who, through his own nature, indeed manifests in many ways as "Om" and so forth.
Whether internal or external, I bow to the Lord who is Sound.
He who, in the form of a secret linga, bears the mark of the celebrated earth,
and by whom the living beings within the cosmic egg are always united.
I bow to the supreme Lord of the anus (Pāyvīśvara), who is most delightful and has arisen as the ultimate; for from whom the various channels (nāḍīs) have each obtained their distinct locations,
and who is the manifest creator of all creations and the sole cause of bliss.
I bow to that Lord of the Mṛḍa-linga and Bhaga, resplendent in His state,
whose single Śakti alone shines forth both in departure and in arrival; I praise that certain, all-pervading One, the Lord of the Foot, who is an ineffable secret.
We always bow to that Lord of Rays, who, resting in the wind, takes up and gives forth [light],
and who is celebrated by his own established nature.
In whomsoever various skill in speech is observed, yet he does not strive for the true meaning through various artificial words, that is mere curiosity.
The multitude of sounds is characterized by the realization of attaining the Supreme Brahman;
Śiva, the Lord of Speech, is beyond the comprehension of even the discerning.
Victorious is this Lord of the Nose, who, though himself mobile, produces through association manifold latent impressions that remain as if stable for a long time in solitude.
Victory to this Lord of Taste (Rasaneśa), who, as if by mere contraction, fashions various kinds of food— both common and principal— and brings them into his own self; he who, through his own skill,
assumes diverse forms within himself alone.

Though situated in the eye, this lord of vision does not see; yet, remaining there, he perceives the touch of objects such as softness and the like. I always bow with supreme reverence to that lord of the skin.
O Lord of the Vedas, we bow to that unborn one, in whom even a multitude of words— though extremely subtle— is generally expanded; he who,
without any other material cause, thus unfolds this entire world.
Let this very mental construction of the visible world shine within the mind.
Victorious is this Prajñeśāna, the sole cause who shines by himself, dispelling the darkness regarding the certainty of existence whether it be far or near;
he before whom the individual soul (jīva), having forgotten its own singular nature, does not remain united with him.
Khelatyu, copinī, covā, mohaṅkāra, and matohara.
Alas, how wonderful it is that he who, having brought the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) under his own control and relying upon the method,
displays his own preeminence in three ways with longing!
The body, like a temple, is defiled by various kinds of impurities and doubts; wander within that temple and realize this Lord of Nature (Prakṛti) who is free from duality.
That which has become dense here attains the state of being composed of light;
that very thing, wandering about, becomes this beautiful, soft sound within the Supreme Person.
May the Lord of Necessity (Niyatīśvara), by whom birth and the rest are determined such that each abandons its own nature, protect us from the miserable states out of his innate compassion.
Victorious is this Lord of Time, who alone, by his own power, measures everything— both internally and externally— without even a subtle atom.
Wandering here and there, it does not depart from its single true source;
amidst existence and non-existence, like flowers, this is some kind of six-legged living being.
He who, though his own course is severed, attains attachment and is hidden everywhere—even in whatever place that may be; we bow to Him, the Lord of Passion.
Victorious is this Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśāna), by whose power the Knower of All (Sarvajña), having abandoned that eternal state of limited awakening, attains it.
When this person reaches a state free from the conceit of being a limited agent, then, alas,
though he is the creator of all, he is but a mere speck within the power of Māyā.
Like a gourd, this living being is carried from here and there;
if it were not for effort, it would simply go and come again and again.
When even the state of being difficult to accomplish appears as accomplished through its locus,
then that which is independent and supreme is fulfilled in its full extent. That which shines with a radiant face here, within all phenomena, drinks them in.
We praise that Māyā, the mistress of the world, who possesses extraordinary arts and splendors.
One should dissolve the "I" into the "not-I," and likewise the "this" into the "not-this.
That which is the expansion of the essence of consciousness, possessing the highest flavor of reality,
is the illuminator illuminated by the radiance of the nature of one's own absolute, singular consciousness.

Possessing a certain, intensely radiant form composed of one and many aesthetic arts and times, appearing through its state of non-reliance as the supreme essence of wonder, it is of the nature of the one, perfectly autonomous Consciousness by means of this supreme [power].

Having resorted solely to that which vibrates as the nature of the thirty-six or thirty principles, one should contemplate one's own state— that which is to be contemplated— which transcends the sphere of both existence and non-existence.
Even while acting through internal power, Śiva remains one whose supreme majesty is uncreated;
O Jayā, he brings about delusion within those who are devoted to the supreme Self as being Śiva.
Dissolution and emergence: where there is dissolution, there is Śiva and Śakti;
for there is Śiva, and you, and I, and even I alone, and where there is neither "I" nor "not-I."
Whose infinite expansion has arisen, who is beyond the calculation of expansion,
who is devoid of even a fraction of any object, and who appears as no object at all— [to him I bow].
Even unity appears as if manifold, or the effect appears as the nature of the cause;
where knowledge shines like ignorance, or where action is actionless;
where even light is darkness, and reflective awareness is non-awareness.
Even the appearance of a stainless jewel shines forth there as something non-existent.

He who shines as higher than the highest, having cast aside Śiva and the rest, devoid of appearances, and having conquered the conceptualization of Śakti and the other [principles], has discarded the state of being the Tattvas and so forth.
He is the remainder of all remainders without exception; he possesses distinctions that are without distinction;
he is devoid of worldly joy, yet he is the bliss of all, like a serpent gliding through the entirety of bliss.

The principle (naya) is the locus for the occurrence and non-occurrence of events such as the cat and the jar; however, there is no extent of a principle that does not also constitute a standpoint (kathaṃcit).
He who is both dependent and independent, who is without characteristics yet the very definition of characteristics,
who is without characteristics because of his possession of all characteristics, and who shines even when he has ceased to exist.
He is the speaker of ever-higher speech, the one who withdraws all that is spoken;
having abandoned both the state of being the object of speech and the state of being the speaker, he shines forth even while relying upon them.
He who shines forth, having adopted an exceedingly graceful style that is neither entirely unified nor divided, nor yet both unified and divided.
He is entirely everything, yet not like the wind; he is difficult to discern because he is beyond the reach of thought and its objects.
He is neither unthought nor thought, for he does not appear as an object; he is the one who brings about liberation through absolute release.
I bow to that supreme Śiva, who is both incomplete and complete, neither empty nor non-empty, devoid of destruction and name, and who is neither anyone at all nor anyone at all.
Transparent, spontaneously fulfilled, it is the state of the fullness of the utterly empty.
Caressing the one who is active, Śiva, who is devoted to the Lord, conquers delusion.
I bow to that self-witnessing one, who here consists of the thirty-six principles and the seven internal measures, and whose very nature is this [reality] itself.
We bow to the Mātṛkā, who is the state of poverty, celebrated as purity, the conscious Lord (cid-īśvara) endowed with wisdom and the power that does not depend on its own bliss.
I, who am devoted to the Mothers, bow to that celebrated Maheśāna, the Mother-mantra, who shines upon the path of Sadāśiva.
I bow to you, the Lord of Mantras, who are consecrated by the mantra of consciousness;
the omniscient one, established in the supreme state of my own sovereign abode.
We praise that which, in the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), takes the form of mantra along with the lords of mantra;
which consists of seventy million [syllables] and grants the fulfillment of all desires, ever-risen.
Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā, and above Māyā is Mayiśva; having saluted Naumi, one should look down upon Śuddhavidyā, which is below Vijñānākala and consists of the Mātṛkās.
O Lord, you sport within Māyā as the Pralayākala and other subjects;
having withdrawn the limbs of the universe, I bow to that wonderful You.
May that all-encompassing Lord be victorious, who abides pervading everything from Puruṣa down to the earth, and who is skilled in the various arts of play.
I bow to You, that Supreme Lord, who— while the fire of consciousness blazes within one's own subjectivity— offers the oblations of objects of knowledge into that very flame.

The means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—who appear as many though they are not manifold; who is the undecaying, singular master within his own body; that Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Wherever I bow to him, he is fully present with a gracious mind;
he is supremely skilled in removing the sleep of delusion.
Aham, aham! Salutation to me; thou art Aho, and salutation to thee as well.
Thou art indeed in my place, and I am likewise in thy place.
Neither I, nor you, nor he, nor even night shines there;
yet where it does shine, we bow to that Supreme Lord.
We praise the Lord who is exceedingly beautiful, who is not exclusively one-sided,
who is not partial, who is lovely, who is the beloved of all, who is not the beloved of anyone [in a worldly sense], and who is the truly desirable Master.
One whose resolve is free from the notion of "I" and "mine," whose latent impressions regarding the living soul and so forth have vanished,
who perceives the true nature of both the world and the non-world, and who is devoted to You— such a person is preeminent.

Victorious is this devotee of yours, who has gone everywhere yet has not gone anywhere; whose mind perceives that which is to be traversed as already traversed; and who has leaped over the very nature of the world.
May this person of yours be honored by all the learned without exception, may they be freed from the contraction of their vision,
and may he increase your great bliss moment after moment.

May he who possesses the sovereignty of devotion to you— whose radiant splendor is his own playful manifestation, who is beyond time, conceptualization, and the net [of illusion], and who has reached the further shore of the supreme— be ever victorious.
One who is intensely eager to taste the nectar of the mass of bliss arising from Your vibration shines forth,
having transcended all boundaries and being solely intent upon You alone.
Is this actor of his own drama born as anyone else? Having attained the state of supreme bliss that is not to be communicated to others, he remains here as something distinct.
Whirled about by the excellent, repeated gusts of the essence of supramundane aesthetic flavor,
this one— though knowing the immeasurable as the measurable— is victorious as a liberated soul.
Devoid of all worldly attire and not resorting to any dress at all,
moving everywhere yet beyond conventional conduct, I, who am liberated while living, am victorious.
Having cast away the four bolts, knowing the mind, straight-minded and consisting of consciousness,
he— though situated within the body from the anus to the crown of the head— is not possessed of a body.
Skilled in the arts of worldly convention, he has reached the state of his own true abode;
he is the consumer of all and yet devoid of food, knowing his own limbs within all limbs.
And you, O Veśamahānanda, reeling from the intoxication of the nectar of ambrosia—
transcending the universe, abiding in the universe, and being the universe itself— this one is victorious!
O dear one, like you, he too conquers, possessing all auspicious splendors;
with a gracious mind, dwelling in heaven, he repeatedly gladdens those who have taken refuge in him.

Having accomplished what was to be done, yet remaining as one who has nothing further to do through the state of having performed all duties; having abandoned both good and evil deeds, this one, liberated while living, is victorious.
Victory to you, O Lord whose splendor is kindled by the play of your own self; victory, O infinite Lord of Light!
Victory to you, whose majesty is untouched by the suffering of others, even while dwelling in the abode of Yama!
Victory to you, O Lord, who are the cause for attaining the state free from affliction, and whose fame consists of the abundance of supreme bliss and the power of strength! May you be victorious!

Thus, having repeatedly praised Maheśa— who had manifested his own glory through the power of the descent of his grace— and while praising him moment by moment, [he remained] according to his play, according to his worldly conduct, and according to...
Following that which has been attained, one who delights in supreme bliss,
perceiving the light of the Self within the self,
and whose nature is free from the various states of worldly existence, transcends the delusion arising from existence and the humiliation of Māyā and other such powers.

Experiencing everywhere a singular descent into all things, yet manifesting manifold splendors, he directly realizes a supreme sovereignty that is to be honored by all beings; though solitary, he moves as if manifold, liberated from bondage and truly free.

A liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta), whose mind is radiant with supreme awakening, crosses the ocean of saṃsāra itself— free from the waves of otherness— coloring it with the stage of supreme passion, while remaining undisturbed by worldly desires for this world or that.
Attaining another state of being through each successive form of compassion, he triumphs as he gazes upon all people as if they were his own kinsmen.

For him, there is nothing whatsoever; all delusion, whether collective or individual, has been dispelled. Even while engaged in activities such as eating and drinking, he proceeds with great ease, having attained the state of one who is free from agency.
Though he is supremely pure, he is graced by the charm of the playful abundance of vast and stainless bliss. This is because—

To him, who by some inexplicable chance has become the source of fear and delusion for everyone, who has made the entire universe his own kingdom, and who wanders about performing his own jests— though he appears in a mild form to someone, somewhere, at some time, and in some way, yet he is seen as something distinct from the disciplined.

Upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, which consists solely of the bliss of the direct realization of one's own Self, and having abandoned the body that remains as a mere vestige of all residual afflictions (*kleśa*), he becomes liberated while in the body (*videhamukta*) and rests in some extraordinary world of his own, in his own innate state— a place devoid of all progeny and free from passion. Upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha*.
But that which is self-revealed, whose nature is beyond another, devoid of ascent and descent, perfected everywhere,
in every way, at all times, and from all sides— by the cessation of delusion regarding that, it is supreme.

Experiencing through the delusion of tranquility the radiance of another, he cultivates each and every state whose nature is unharmed by joy and sorrow; and perfuming all existence with a song of pure being as a universal essence, or rather, with the supreme latent impression (*vāsanā*).

With the latent impressions of the fruits of actions being performed already purged, he remains as one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), abiding in his own place—which is actually placeless—as the supreme state itself. Though appearing to remain within *saṃsāra*, he is as if not remaining there, with all fear and doubt regarding Yama and other such powers dissolved. And of these two, [the first is] the one liberated while living, and [the second is] the one liberated after death (*videhamukta*).
Although both were alive, possessed of equal power, and had reached the same level of status, and although both directly perceived the entire creation of the Grandfather (Brahmā) as their own,

this much distinction alone remained superior between those two who possessed the fame of being the most refined of men and who had established their dwellings on opposite shores of the shoreless ocean.

In one [state], one's own bliss has dissolved into a single point and remains as something defined like water poured out from a vessel; for the other, however, his steps toward the experience of the Supreme proceed again and again— how can such a thing even be described?
What kind of person is he who, while suddenly relishing his own greatness, wanders upon the path highly honored by the great? He is indeed that very play of bliss;
like the waters of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) flowing everywhere, whom does he not delight by dispelling all delusion through his extraordinary gait?
By means of salutation, by means of honoring, by means of accumulation, by means of refinement, by means of turning back from corruption, and by means of supreme assistance.

And for this very one who is liberated while living— who wanders through the world, which though essence-less is yet the essence of all— what is not experienced by all people through their service and veneration, as he proceeds to the higher and lower worlds?
The state of being a purifier for the three types of families, whether they are transformed by good deeds or evil deeds;
the state of being the progenitor of all; the purity of the earth; the acquisition of abundant fame; and mastery.

The excellence [of this] consists in the merit of bathing in all other sacred fords, the granting of the entire earth as a gift, the status of being a master and guru by one's own nature, the performance of thousands of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, the attainment of sovereignty over the celestial realms,
and the propitiation of all the lords of the immortals.

Through gold, jewels, and other such things that never lose their brilliance, there is nourishment for victory and the constant attainment of success; indeed, by following that unerring path, one finds delight in every condition, in every way, and at all times, even though [the world] is subject to decay.

The maintenance of the three debts of the body is supreme and infinite; it is the excellent covering of the mouth, noble exertion again and again, the practice of conduct that captivates the hearts of people,
lords of men, and others, the performance of pure actions, and the removal of minor offenses, sins, and great transgressions.
Adorned with the most diverse ornaments, the refuge of wretched people,
the supreme playground of all wonders, O Supreme Lord, the mutual resort at every moment, the forgetting of the existence and non-existence of all things— in that most excellent state.
It is the cause for stability in one's own state, the dispeller of fear from the low and the high, the remover of delusions such as death, and the uplifter to supreme bliss; moreover,
its most excellent nature is free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence.

Free from delusion and agitation, possessing the conceit of being a living soul yet remaining a living-soul even beyond the state of a living soul, and a non-living soul that is utterly more pure than a living-non-living soul; he whose intention is to bestow the splendor of divine play upon all living beings, who is himself desireless, and who is worthy of salutation by Brahmā and the other gods.

O Sudarśana, who is beyond the *stotra* and *vaṣaṭ* calls; who is devoid of the impurity of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); who is the sovereign glory of the Supreme, presiding over the sacrifice of sovereignty over all worlds; who is free from every limitation; who is the supreme teacher of all teachers; O Great Non-dual Śiva, Non-dual Brahman!
O Sudarśana, that which is to be realized through supreme cultivation is experienced in the visions of Sudarśana;

it is inferred by its movement in the lower visions; it is desired as an attainable goal in the visions permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and so forth; and it is sung of in other visions.
And as for the distinction between what is possible and what is impossible, what is past, future, or present— for one who proceeds everywhere devoid of the conceit of agency,
there is a manifestation in its entirety through the inherent grace of that which unfolds.

By transcending the states of mind that are both appropriate and inappropriate, he alone sustains the earth as its supporter; by his very tongue, which has revealed the state of being a cow (the earth), even the water possesses ever-fresh flavor and life;
and by his mere glance, it becomes radiant with splendor—this indeed belongs to him alone.
By his mere touch, even the wind became as if disciplined; and by the utterance of his words alone,
the sky— though empty, infinite, and renowned for its qualities of sound— was illuminated on all sides by the radiance of the luminous ones and was being purified.
For him, by whom all meditative cultivation has been dissolved, by whom the cultivation of other states has been dissolved,

and by whom the existence of meditative cultivation— which causes the confusion of higher and lower states through the cultivation of others— has been dissolved through cultivation and thorough discernment, there are gods and non-gods, all gods, the Vedas and the non-Vedas, and the knowable and the unknowable.

Non-Vedas and all Vedas, worlds and non-worlds and all worlds, sacrifices and non-sacrifices and all sacrifices, dharmas and non-dharmas and all dharmas, purposes and non-purposes and all purposes, desires and non-desires and all desires, and those who are free from desire.

Those whose desires are fulfilled are of two kinds: those possessing fruits and those possessing non-fruits; likewise, there are those who are liberated, those who are not liberated, those who are completely liberated, and those whose liberation is total liberation. She is the mother, yet not the mother, and the mother of all;
he is the father, yet not the father, and the father of all; he is the brother worthy of respect, yet not the brother, and the brother of all.

She is both a sister and not a sister, she is both everything and not everything, and she is both a daughter and not a daughter, she is the daughter of all; he is both a son and not a son, and he is the son of all; he is both a kinsman and not a kinsman, and he is the kinsman of all; the perfected ones, beginning with the grandfathers of all, are both perfected and not perfected, and they are the perfection of all; and time is not time.
Time and all time; direction and non-direction, all directions and non-direction, all places and non-place;
form and non-form, every form and non-form;
something and nothing, everything and something—the perfection of all, the perfection of perfection, the perfection of the perfection of perfection.

Through the attainment of the supreme self-perfection of this [Lord], everything is not-everything, yet for Him it is the totality of all things; and by the wandering of His very own playful manifestation, there are all the continents: Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmalī, and Gomedha.
Likewise, there are the regions known as Puṣkara and Jambudvīpa,
and the countries situated within them, such as Kaśmīra, Kīra, Darada, Abhimāra, Taṅgaṇa, Kulūta, Kuṇaṭa, Khaśa, Ghoṣa, Kaca, Cika, Dārva, Dāmara, Kirāta, Cīna, Mahācīna, and others as well.
The regions of Brahmakārvaṭa, Paṇḍravaṇa, Magadha, and Mithilā;
Prāgjyotiṣa, Bhadra, Gauḍa, and Pauṇḍra;
and various places such as Oṭkalika, Āsaya, Mekalā, Ambaṣṭha, Komalaka, and Kāvardhamāna.
Others as well— Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Upavaṅgas, Jaṭharāṅgas, Mūlikas, Vidarbhas, Vatmāndhras,
Vaidikas, Vaṣatrīs, Purīśālas, Kiṣkindas, Niṣādas, Purikas, Daśārṇas, Nakhādya, and other Kaṅkaṭas.
Kaṅkaṇa, Śivikābhīra, Kaṅkaṇaga, Nanda, Kerala, Karṇāṭaka, Āñcī, Deśamarucī, Paṭṭhāna, Siṃhalaka, Chādyā, and others such as Pahlava,
Kāmboja, Sindhu, Sauvīra, Arava, Ambaṣṭha, Kapila, Yavana, Śūdra, Barbara, and Kirāta.
Muṇḍa, Ābhīra, Muñjaka, Kālaka, Surāṣṭra, Bādara, Raivataka, Mukhya, Ajapara, Kaṣāntaka, Urukaṇa, Pañcanada, Rāmaṭha, Vaiśyataka, Nirmaryāda, Śaka, and Mleccha.
There were others as well, such as those who subsisted on the bulbs found in hoof-prints,
and those devoted to the Māṇḍavyas, Bhutkhāras, Tālahalas, Haḍas, and so forth; and also the Kokalakas, Kekayas, Vasātayas, Trigartas, and Śātakas.
Also [the lands of] Māṇḍavya, Ambara, Madraka, Mālava, Paurava, Gāndhāra, and others; Ājapya, Bhadra, Ari, Medha, Sālva, Nīpa, Ujjihāna, Maru,
Vāṭadhāna, Vatsa, Yāmuna, Sārasvata, Mādhyamika, Māthūra, Kaśmīra, Śūra-sena, Pāṇḍu, and Pāñcāla.

Sāketa, Hastināpura, and others; furthermore, the various specific regions such as Aṅga and so forth; likewise, the great rivers and streams such as the Kṣārā and their tributaries; and other diverse territories situated within these intervals.

By taking hold of this very state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta-daśā), the worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, as well as the subterranean worlds beginning with Pātāla, are purified, sustained, and transcended by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Agni.

The hosts of principal deities, beginning with Samavarti, Rasarāja, Pavanarāja, Rājarāja, and Śaṅkara; the celestial sages such as Nārada, Marīci, Pulaha, Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, and others; and the Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras—[all these were present].
Siddhas, Sādhyas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Apsarases, gods, spirits, and others of divine origin,
as well as great ṛṣis such as Dattātreya, Vyāsa, Jābāli, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu, Bharadvāja, Kautsa, Upamanyu, Yājñavalkya, Durvāsas, Kaṇṭha, Uttaṅka, Sumedhas, and Jaimini.
Gautama, Harikeśa, Śṛṅganāsika, Ketu, Kauśika, Uddālaka, Śaṅkhalikhita, and other leading lords of men, such as Pṛthu, Nṛga, Manu, Ikṣvāku, Daśaratha, Raghu, Bharata,
Kuru, Pāṇḍu, Daśaratha, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna.
Kuśa, Pāṇḍu, Śūrasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Nakula, Sahadeva, Uddhava, Akrūra, Śikhidhvaja, and others, as well as the foremost among the Dānavas, such as Bali and Prahlāda.

Paraśurāma and others who are long-lived; Śrī Bhagavān Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna together with their devotees; Sītā, Mandodarī, Kṛṣṇā, Tārā, Ahalyā, Anasūyā, Lopāmudrā, and other jewels among women; as well as the Gāyatrī, Sarvamaṅgalā, and others.

O Lord of gods, [I offer salutations] to Śrī, Śacī, Prabhā, and other foremost divine and excellent women; to Kumāra, Gaṇanāyaka, Vaṭuka, Bhairava, and others; and to Kāmeśa and other divine lovers, according to their respective activities and as they appear.

Other supreme beings as well— gods, asuras, serpents, and eminent humans, including all the serpent kings such as Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka— have attained, are attaining, and will attain this abode, which is the non-dual vibration of the universal existence of supreme bliss.

They find complete satisfaction through the supreme vision of this very one who is liberated while living. Thus, this one liberated while living is the Supreme Lord Śiva himself; by means of Śivā as the instrument, for the sake of Śiva, from Śiva, of Śiva—within that very Śiva, the supreme self, he perceives his own transcendence.
Oṃ! Being self-luminous, beyond nourishment, and indeed beyond even the mind, Śiva has been, is becoming, and will be. Oṃ.

Thus, this glorious Kalpapādapa (Wish-Fulfilling Tree) composition— bound by bonds, the bond of bondage, the binding of bondage, the wealth of the means for attainment, beginning with the Great Non-duality,
O Sudarśana, Sudarśana, Sudarśana, Sudarśana!— is the venerable great sage Kaśyapa.
Composed by the one named Śrīmacchrīmāhibhakaula—

who has established his presence in the land of Kaśmīra, the supreme cause of the Satīsarovara lake which is the ultimate excellence of all regions, fashioned by the wind, and possessed of the great majesty of absolute sovereignty; and who is the most stainless [work] produced by the breeze.
By no one other than Śiva— who is the supreme architect, beautifully fashioned with branches, fruits, flowers, and trunks composed of consciousness— was he created;
he was the illustrious sovereign of the distinguished land of Śrīmaruvāṭa, an embodiment of supreme knowledge.

By me, who am impelled by the Great King of Kings, the Universal Monarch named Praṇunnena-mayāsatā-paramakāruṇyavatumukṣāvat-āsuphala, whose memory of the far shore of the boundless ocean of this essence-less saṃsāra has been purified— [this work is composed] for those seeking liberation.
Then, while residing in the middle country (*madhyadeśa*), she looked toward the favor of the powerful;

and in the illustrious Śrī-Vikramāditya Śaka, which is reckoned from the time of Rāma, Agni, and the Moon, and in the illustrious Śālivāhana Śaka measured by the Vasus (8), Aṅkas (9), Rāmas (3), and Jīvātṛkas (14)— that is, 8931— [she was] in Kaśmīra.
And according to the movement of the Seven Sages (Ursa Major), in a year measured by the arrows of the eyes (two thousand five hundred), in the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas,
on the lunar day presided over by Viṣṇu, joined with Monday, and in the Siddhi Yoga;

On the birthday of his own son named Śrīmacchīnātha Kaula, during an advanced stage of the supreme yoga (parayoga), while the moon was situated in the sign of Virgo (vanitārāśi) at the time of its rising, and while the sun was occupying the sign of Leo (siṃharāśi) in its own domicile.

On the day marking the commencement of the rains by the son of Rohiṇī (the Moon), garlanded with a thousand rays (the Sun), in the twelfth cycle of five-year periods, in the year presided over by Bhaga, known as Pañcamābdhita-dhvatsara,
and in the sixtieth year from Prabhava onwards, presided over by Śiva.

In the year 2177 of the Kali Yuga, when the illustrious Vāsuki, the king of the Nāgas, was the lord of the year; while the son of the Sun (Saturn) was the preeminent minister and the son of the Earth (Mars) had attained the status of sovereign; and while the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) was the lord of the month—the rainy season—[this occurred].
And in the case of the merchant’s wife Bhagavatī and Rohiṇī, this Kalānidhi, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree, brought his playful and most beautiful composition to its conclusion.

This work is the composition of Śrīman Śrī Kṛṣṇakaula, who is the manifestation of the glory of the supreme realization of the Self of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; he is the son of the mother named Buddhi— a veritable ocean of compassion and the very embodiment of wisdom—
and is the delight of his affectionate parents, Ananta and Sudarśanā.

O Sudarśana, [you who are] the younger brother of the Sudarśanakaulas, O Siddheśvara, [you who are] the foremost among the Siddhakaulas, O you who are a single mass of unbroken consciousness and bliss, Śiva himself, [you whose] maternal grandfather and supreme guru are the illustrious Śivarājānaka!
The essence of Śrīvidyā, Śrī Śrī Śrī Śrī [Śrīnāthavara,
Śrīhetunātha, and Śrījñānasvāmin], who have recognized their own innate, supreme Self through the compassionate glance of grace— [this is] forty-seven years.

This work, which brings delight to virtuous persons such as Śrīnātha Mallā and others, belongs to the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Sahib Kaulapāda, whose fame is celebrated through compositions such as the *Śrīgāyatrībhāṣya* and the *Śrīdevīnāmavilāsa*.
Auspiciousness.
